2.7: Reconvene

>>Present a logical argument for why you're not a thief.

>>Yes, because you wanted an adult's advice how to handle these situations.

-Emphasize that you only want advice, not for them to take action in return due to the risk.

EXP: 125/130

Mood: Awful.

This isn't the first time you've been accused of stealing property, and it certainly won't be the last, which is why you are able to put down your chopsticks, fold your hands in your lap, and affix Pelte with a flat stare.

"What?" she growls.

"What, what?" You repeat, raising your eyebrows.

"Did you steal the boss's rubix cube or not?"

[Logic check: 55/40 -> Success! +5 EXP.]

You cock your head. You give Pelte a mild grin. You speak in the smooth, confident tone that one American businesswoman used in her movie when laying the facts upon a board of directors.

"I'm going to lay it out to you straight, Pelte. One: I have literally zero reason to steal something from my roommate's shelf. She sleeps half a meter away from me. Two: I'm not the type of uma who does that, because I have ears, and they're telling me I'm on thin enough ice as it is around these parts."

"Well, at least you—"

"Thirdly." You interject, raising your voice a notch on the volume scale. "Have you seen what Tabaru's sisters are made of?"

That sets the record straight. Pelte gulps. She leans back in her seat and huffs. Other pairs of ears on her two friends shoot up. You just nod and let the implications stew. A gambler, a yakuza, a tyrant, a scary policewoman, Tracen's own Terrorist of the Racetrack (you saw the footage of Narita Top Road's crash, and boy did it look and sound nasty), and Gold Ship. You'd rather hold a picnic on the freeway. And while you're on this tangent, judging how Pelte's cheeks are rapidly paling, you presume she's been invited for a 'chat' as the only member of Tabaru's hometown league to make it to nationals. High standards extend to a family member's friends, right?

"Golshi probably took it." Tabaru speaks up.

"Pardon?" You say.

"The Spica sack monster…" Jewel mumbles, shivering. She is ignored.

Tabaru fidgets with her phone between bites of her chicken sandwich. She flips the device around, showing LANE. "Yep, Golshi just sent me a message. Said she found that I dropped it somewhere and instead of returning it to me, she borrowed it for a super important special project. We'll find out from the bleachers on the track next week."

It will involve an explosion. Sugar, clouds, sugar clouds—who knows? The two of you lock eyes and agree on this. Umamusume solidarity.

"So." You say, "I didn't steal it."

"Nope." Tabaru replies. "You didn't. I probably left it lying around somewhere, and Golshi snatched it up."

"There." You face Pelte with a hint of smugness. "Your boss says so. Are we done here?"

Pelte shoves a spoonful of fried rice into her mouth and glances away. "I'm still keeping an eye on you."

You shrug. Whatever.

[+1 to Lawful Alignment. Overall Alignment did not shift.]

"Yeah, yeah, just stalk her like some creep while you're at it." Tomoe says, with an exaggerated shrug that morphs into a grin full of good humor. "Geez, Ruby, when did you grow a spine? Maybe you'll stick around for real."

You'd answer that you had always possessed a spine. Competition in the underground is fierce. Hearts get shattered with every update of the rankings list. It's entirely possible to sing your heart out, receive a smattering of applause and no other rewards at all. There are enough tales in you about this topic to write a book, or at least several comprehensive and detailed blog posts on tomorrowisfaithful.net/blog, the official news coverage for Shibuya's up-and-coming underground enka group.

Right now, you're keeping your mouth shut. No, it's not because you don't enjoy talking about this topic. It's more to do with the bundle of pressure coalescing in the seat next to you.

"Tomoe, you moron! Why did you go and say that?"

"I didn't know. I thought enough time—it was a joke!"

Tabaru is a quiet uma. She acts like she's counting cards in a casino when the rest of the table plays Go Fish. People exchange words and come out thinking she's lost in her own world, or that she's piercing their soul with her gaze. Outwardly, this is true. Behind that standoffish disposition lies a composed, generally well-being girl who only speaks when she feels like there's something worth talking about. In an age where the Internet shrinks attention spans and news flies off the shelves past the speed of sound, that's a gift you can appreciate.

You'd be remiss, as you're being reminded now, to forget that Tabaru is a member of the Gold Clan. The lunacy of Gold Ship, Dream Journey, Orfevre and the rest of her clan dwells with her. It's manifesting in front of you as raw severity.

"Boss!" Jewel crumbles under Tabaru's glare. Cold as stone, nary a spark in those round eyes. "It was a joke. A joke. I didn't mean it—"

"I know, Jewel. Please don't bring that up again." Tabaru replies. A sharp crack. The chopsticks splinter in her grip. Tabaru tosses them off to the side with nary a glance.

[(Guts check: 8/9 || Tabaru's Social Link >= 1) -> Sucess! +5 EXP.]

"What's this about?" You ask.

That intense, dark look Tabaru wears lands itself on you. Your neck goes stiff, ears ceasing their twitching. Jewel takes the opportunity to slouch back in her seat and bury herself in slurping up her miso soup.

"My old roommate. She disappeared one day. Didn't even leave a note." Tabaru's says tersely. "She should have."

"I'm sorry to hear that. I hope she's doing okay, wherever she is."

Tabaru grimaces. She returns to her meal, glaring down at her plate. "She promised to win a G2. Only a G2."

"Only, she says…" Pelte mumbles.

Out of the thousands upon thousands of umamusume that run in high-stakes competition, only a fraction of those make it to the G2 level, never mind winning them. A G2 victory, therefore, is not the worst choice for a lifelong dream.

Tabaru resumes eating her sandwich, and the conversation disintegrates. You might have revived it, reassured Tabaru, asked for more details about this predecessor of yours. It wasn't her fault her old roommate vanished out of nowhere, because Tabaru isn't the kind of rambunctious troublemaker to raise hell for Hishi Amazon or the rest of the dorm. A couple of old acquaintances from the music business jumped ship for other opportunities or were forced to quit. You may have cried a little in the early stages. Kaede took you aside and gently informed you that this was a fact of life. What you're struggling to get to is that you can relate.

Heck, that Fukukitaru uma had her old client disappear on her. There's a connection. A story.

[(Instinct: 23/50 || World Resonance: 50/50) -> Success. +10 EXP.]

A chill in your fingertips, like sticking your hand in a winter-cold pond. A stray finger wraps around your silver bullet. This is some coincidence.

Then, you brush it off, because a hunch is just that without anything happening. And you remain quiet—again—because you are not normal Ruby but rather miffed and displeased Ruby who is cursing her good memory. A bridge beneath Fuchu's morning light, a trip down the many lanes of the big city, the appearance of Oguri Cap, My Big Body, a fridge full of carrots. Satono Diamond and Kitasan Black. An invitation. Hesitation quashed in favor of pure, blind hope. The sweet cakes that stained your teeth, and the blanked attempts at conversation. The olive branch, the gouging, the spite, the refusal, the begging and pleading and the hate seeping from the thousands of pores of your former sister's beautiful features—

You whip your right hand out. You take the bottle of orange juice, unscrew the cap and chug and wish the sweet-sour taste washes the past weekend away. It almost does. Almost.

You can't hide from the truth. It's been consuming your thoughts for the past few days. The electronic signs above shops in Shinjuku are less invasive.

Diamond despises you. Crown, maybe just as much. They hate the fact that you stole your mother's shoes and ran away; that you successfully applied and enrolled in Tracen; that you still hold love for your own mother despite the crime she committed. You're unsure what a normal response to this counts, either. Cry your eyes out? You did that plenty on the day, then later at night while cradling your mother's shoes and burying your face in your pillow. Pretend nothing happened? Impossible. You're acknowledging that a thing happened. Get mad and swear vengeance like an ancient hero of myth?

Maybe. Somewhere amidst the tears wept until the eve of midnight, you felt a spike of anger. An urge to strike your pillow and imagine the center was Diamond's dainty little nose. How dare she drag you to that stupid coffee palace and lead you on? How dare she demand the last token you have of your mother's existence? You opened your heart, and she took a knife and stabbed you in the gut!

She…

She used to be so sweet and kind. That part of her is still there—you heard how she giggled with Kitasan Black—but it's no longer for you. Now you're miserable again and also faintly jealous of Kitasan Black. What does she have that you don't? At least Kitasan didn't yell at her alongside Diamond.

"Oi, Ruby." Tabaru taps you on the shoulder. "Lunch time's over."

"Oh." You blink. "Yeah, it sure is. Coming…"

The day passes. Your bad mood persists, a real storm cloud over the horizon. It's so bad you zone in and out of class; the teacher calls your name, and you panic to bundle together an answer for the maths question. That's when you decide this has gone too far. Ruminating by yourself was useless. Grass Wonder and Oguri Cap can only tend to your feelings so much. No, what you need is rock-solid advice. There's only one adult whom you can turn to.

That afternoon, you climb up to the academy roof, find a spot in the shade, and punch in the number.

"Ana-Fabulous Offices, this is Mr. Suzuki speaking. How may I help you?"

"It's me, boss."

"Ruby." An exhale of breath, belonging to a masculine tone with the texture of a gravel driveway. It's a product of smoking too much at after-work parties before slamming on the brakes and going cold turkey. You hear papers rustling and the mild metallic grinding of a laptop pushed aside. "You sound flustered. Tell me about it."

It's been several months, yet your ex-manager still recognises the sound of your distress. Why wouldn't he? Manager Suzuki isn't demented, or anything. A sense of ease washes over you, the muscles holding your tail up softening. Your imagination drifts, and you're sitting on that hard plastic chair in his office, the flat-screen second monitor buzzing in the background, a fresh circle in red marker on the group's latest appointment on the nearby calendar. On his desk: his nameplate, the photo of the kids, the rubber ducky Hotaru brought him as a joke present, and the view of the street below with its 24-hour convenience store and neighbouring thrift shop and the sights and smells that are distinctly urban and FAITHFUL. He's almost certainly wearing that gaudy orange tie Madame Sugar tossed at him, too.

A pang in your heart. You missed this. There's no time to reminisce, because Manager Suzuki is a busy man with forms to fill out and four other girls to wrangle. You refrained from badgering him about your previous problems at Tracen for that reason. He's not the type to say A and secretly mean B; you've been given a full pass to spill, so you do.

Manager Suzuki listens in complete silence. He's paying attention. Were you face to face, he'd be nodding along, his hands firmly resting on his knees.

"Please don't tell the other girls about this." You say upon finishing your recollections.

"Too late. They're peeking around the corner. I'm going to be interrogated the moment I step outside my office." You imagine him glowering past his phone, waving one thick hand in the universal sign of 'get lost'. "They will want to help you too."

You shudder. "Hotaru and Kaede will go on the warpath. I don't want to distract you guys with my personal troubles. You must all be so busy."

"There are few umamusume singers who aren't entrenched in their own groups, and none of them are you." Manager Suzuki remarks.

You smile at that. It doesn't last long.

"So…" You begin hesitantly. "What do you think?"

Another pause. You imagine him furrowing his brows and stroking his chiseled, stubble-lined chin. An odd quirk of human genetics granted your manager an abnormally large height (for a Japanese human man). Jokes have been made comparing him to a walking fridge. Hotaru compared his resting face to a stone statue once. "I think Satono Diamond is far more unpleasant than she appears on the Satono company broadcasts."

"You believe me." You say.

"You're not one to lie, nor act hysterical." He replies. "Do you want my honest opinion of how you handled the talk?"

"Shoot."

"It was an unmitigated disaster."

You wince. Well, you just thought about how he doesn't mince words. You walked right into that one. "What's the silver lining?"

"There's hardly any." Your ex-manager clears his throat. "Ruby, you were absurdly fortunate this hasn't leaked into the public spotlight. The more you talked, the more I anticipated some journalist barging past the gates of the academy and thrusting a microphone into your face. Thankfully, you haven't mentioned that, which means Satono Diamond herself or one of her associates has made efforts to cover the meeting up, since none of us have heard anything from the local news. It's easy for them to release a press statement claiming they will re-educate their heiress. They could even present it as her having a single bad day like any ordinary umamusume."

"I see…"

"In addition, the aftermath has clearly affected your mental state. Your voice shook more than a couple of times, and you held off from calling me until you had time to think and hope that you pushed past it—unsuccessfully, mind you."

You nod. No rebuttal. He's correct. The only thing missing is his favorite whiteboard.

Manager Suzuki sighs. "This is partially my fault."

"It wasn't your responsibility." You reply.

"It was," Manager Suzuki stresses. "It was my duty as an adult. I should have sat you down and advised you about the Satonos."

"And I was in a hurry to leave." You say, and smile weakly. "We were all super busy back then. I threw a real wrench into FAITHFUL's plans, and I was still clinging onto my childhood memories. I probably would have ignored you. Really, I was deluding myself so much.

"You finally discovered Diamond's true feelings. That's the silver lining. Its execution I never would have wished on you."

You sigh. "Same."

Manager Suzuki grunts. "For now, you'll have to avoid them."

He can hear your face fall, see you chew your lip. "Ruby?" He asks, after a pause.

"What if Diamond and Crown come to me?"

"For your mother's shoes?"

"Yeah." One of your nightmares involved them snatching the shoes out of your hands and throwing them atop a pyre back at the shrine.

His response is swift and blunt. "Run."

"What?"

"You heard me. Just run."

There's an irony in a human of all creatures ordering an umamusume to run. You're not focusing on that. Manager Suzuki is using his lecture voice, where he dumps information upon his girls and expects them to pay full attention, because he won't be repeating himself a second time. You scramble to flick aside the phone app and open up a notepad.

"Make up an excuse, cause a distraction, or turn your back to them and walk in the other direction. There is no law the Satonos can wield to force you into a conversation against your will. Your teachers may take issue so simply explain that you will not be harassed by another student. Escalate the situation to the higher academy faculty if you have to, then stay silent until you've gathered enough information and willpower to speak. We live in a democracy where you are not obliged to speak unless you want to. This is an extreme case—Tracen is not the kind of institution that strikes me as being wholly dominated by the Satonos."

These are tactics you could have concluded by yourself. They feel more assured coming from your ex-manager. You catch his implication: this will happen. He's certain of it. He's worked with corporate before. Behind those fine suits and whitewashed smiles lurk some truly doggedly persistent individuals. It's good information, yet it doesn't make you feel good. It's another reminder that your sisters see you as an enemy to be crushed, not a stranger to be befriended.

"Do you remember what I said about time and place?" Manager Suzuki asks.

"Pick our battlefields." You recite. The venue matters. The more comfortable a singer is, the better tunes they'll belt out. The same applies to a negotiation.

"Exactly. Don't go to a coffee palace. Find a nice corner cafe, or a park, or even the academy cafeteria. A neutral zone is better than one that innately rebels against you. Better if you can throw Diamond off, too. Build up your mental resilience and practice speeches. If Tracen offers public speaking classes, attend them and construct arguments on why your mother's legacy does not matter, or whatnot. Keep making friends and see if they're willing to accompany you. I don't think you need me to advise you on that." Manager Suzuki says. You can hear a hint of his smile. "Grass Wonder and Oguri Cap. I'd never have imagined it. Nice work, Ruby."

You preen a little. Rare praise. You speak with enthusiasm. "Grass is the best. She carried me to the infirmary and made sure I was okay afterwards. She personally asked the chefs to prepare me a super big late lunch. I'm so blessed to have met her. Same with Oguri."

Manager Suzuki huffs in amusement. A snerk. "You've hit the jackpot with that one."

"Did I? I know she's famous and the Prez likes her, but her prime was years ago."

"Famous, she says…that's like saying the sun is slightly warm." Manager Suzuki is definitely shaking his head back and forth. He scoffs. "I'll put it like this. Oguri Cap returned to Kasamatsu for her retirement ceremony. An unusual request for the time, I believe, but it happened. Guess how many people showed up."

"Did she fill the stadium?"

"She filled the stadium, alright, and then every single street surrounding it. More attendees than the entire population of Kasamatsu showed up to watch their heroine's final race. This goes far beyond Special Week or Grass Wonder, Ruby. We're talking about an umamusume who rivaled Elvis Presley or Michael Jackson at her peak."

"…wow."

"Wow, indeed."

That's…a lot of bodies jostling together for a glimpse of a single umamusume. Multiple G1 winners receive a ton of attention, but to stretch an entire town past its breaking points is insane. The merch stores must have blown out their stock in minutes.

"But her fame must have waned. She retired. Other umas showed up to take her place, like...I dunno, the Golden Generation, or T.M Opera O?"

"There are still many who think fondly of Oguri Cap. You should not underestimate that level of influence." Manager Suzuki concludes.

"So get her on my side."

"Yes, yes, yes. I'll write it in calligraphy if I have to."

You chuckle. There's an undercurrent of hesitation beneath it. A problem exists: the fact you haven't seen hide nor tail of Oguri since the weekend. It's weird. Usually she's tucked in a corner of the cafeteria chomping down her usual dozen plates of good. Now? She's gone. Vanished into thin air, or at least adjusted her schedule so the two of you don't meet. Is she avoiding you? Surely not. Grass Wonder did mention Oguri had a couple of things to think about, so if you had to theorize, you'd say she's taken time off from the academy.

You won't lie. A barrier exists between the two of you. You're more than willing to connect, so it's entirely on Oguri's side.

[Psyche check: 9/9 -> Success! +10 EXP.]

It might be related to the domineering presence she keeps forcing down your senses' throats. Grass Wonder doesn't exude that, nor did Narita Brian, or even Symboli Rudolf herself.

[Psyche check: 9/11-> Failure.]

You try to come up with a reason on the spot and fail.

The wind picks up. It brushes your hair, then bats you on the cheeks with a mild chill. The sun is setting in the distance, the light of the sky descending from fiery orange to the muted tones of dusk. Soon, a member of the faculty will ascend to the roof and shoo anyone still lounging around. There's one final set of questions you have.

"Is there hope for Diamond?" You ask.

Manager Suzuki grunts. "As in, do you think she can change for the better?"

Heaviness in your throat. You try to force it down. "Yeah."

"You still love her as a sister." Manager Suzuki says, and you can't decide if the sound following it belongs to a grin or a grimace.

"I…do. At least, I think I do. Maybe it's me trying to process what happened and being stuck in denial and whatever, but I still keep thinking back to how Dia used to be, and I'm still finding some level of comfort there? It hurts. It really does, now knowing what she's like. But if she behaved like that before, maybe she can come back?"

"She's a spoiled girl."

"That's…"

"It's a fair assessment of her character. I met those types when I was in sales. Bratty, lavish, entitled souls who believe some early childhood training and their family's credit card can let them get their way with all sorts of ridiculous nonsense." Manager Suzuki says, "She led you on and broke your heart in a calculated mood. I have American acquaintances who would have considered that the final straw. Indeed, if Kaede or Miki or any of the girls did that to me, I'd be showing them the door without hesitation."

There's a hint of staunchness in his tone. You can only sit there and make a soft, "Oh." It's a massive breach of trust. Framed that way, Diamond is unforgivable, irredeemable.

"But…"

You perk up, ears twitching.

"Diamond is a product of the upbringing crafted by the adults surrounding her, who are no longer present now that she's enrolled. She's now obliged to live for several years on neutral ground. She's forced to reconcile with her family's failure to bar you from enrollment. She will make contact with umamusume who are only tangentially or hardly connected to the Satonos. I can't imagine all of them are pleased with the ruckus her family made."

Like Narita Brian, who was harangued by journalists until she snapped in your face. Grass Wonder's not happy either, when you spoke to her in the infirmary. She tried to conceal it for your sake, yet you knew that if Diamond was in the room, and Grass Wonder was holding her naginata, a new patient would've been created on the spot.

"You're saying there's a chance." You say quickly.

Manager Suzuki hesitates, knowing full well the rope of faith is intertwined between your fingers. He can hear you breathing.

"People change, don't they?" You add.

"It will be hard. It will be taxing. It will not be done tomorrow, or at the end of this month, perhaps not even by the time you graduate. You'll be willingly pricking yourself over and over again atop Satono Diamond's thorns."

"But it's not impossible."

He heaves a sigh. "No, it's not. You and her are both children. Children grow up."

Normally, you'd sniff at such a statement of your age. Now, it's a glimpse of pure gold.

"She's been misled by her parents in her life. We're living in a reality where you are not the devil; that she'll be taking head-on. Prepare for the breakdown, Ruby. It will not be pretty." Manager Suzuki says.

You nod again and again. "Thank you, boss. Thank you so much! I totally owe you one."

"No, you don't," Manager Suzuki concludes. "Like I said, this is my duty as an adult. If you're really willing, I wouldn't say no to hearing you sing again."

A shout in the background. It sounds faintly of Kaede, telling him to get his ass up and move along. She's the only one who can do that as the eldest in this gaggle of misfits. Manager Suzuki excuses himself, you nod and smile and tell him to send the other members your best regards, and the conversation ends.

You lean against the wall. You review the last…twenty minutes? Sheesh, that took a while. The more you sit there and soak in your ex-manager's words, the more the mire of uncertainty you were flailing about in clears up. It hardens into a flat, terse sensation. It's not happiness, nor is it sadness. It's…pure relief. Yes. Yes, that's exactly what it is. Relief and resolve. Manager Suzuki is many things. Blunt, strict with his girls, consumes too much konbini sushi, a bit of a prude whenever Hotaru decides to wear outfits that show off a bit of skin…but he's never misled his talents, you included. If he says reconciling with Diamond is possible, then it is.

You're not crazy. Your fragile hope is not crazy. Bless your ex-manager's heart, too. That's why he's an adult you respect, unlike those two-faced priests back at the shrine.

A purification ritual, my tail.

You find yourself curling up in a ball again, the same as when you woke up in the infirmary, except this time you're not hiding your face, and you are no longer wet with tears. Your stomach instead clenches with determination. There are plans forming in your head. Avenues of action you can take. They're outlandish and frayed and a tad disconnected from reality, but they're a start. One day, Diamond might see the light. Her and Crown and even the rest of the Satonos!

...well, maybe not them, assuming what your ex-manager said was true. The upper Satono conglomerate fed those lies to your sister-cousins. They're the ones you'll be angry at. Yeah, that checks out.

For now: the try-outs. The track should be open for ten more minutes of jogging.

As you lift your head and gaze into the descending sunset, you wonder if this is what it means to grow up.

What's the best method of keeping a troublesome prisoner locked away?

That's simple, you might say. Confine them to a cell. Chain their legs to the wall, and then lock the door shut. Deprive them of light, both natural and artificial, save for a single slot in the wall from which bread and water will be deposited, as cameras affixed to the ceiling observe them with night vision so high up they might as well be in another building.

There's no way to escape. No space to do anything of significance. The prisoner is secure.

Ah, but there's still an issue. Read my question again. We're not talking about an ordinary prisoner. We're talking about a troublesome prisoner, remember. Those are the ones who can and have endured the world's cruelty and are more than ready to dish out some of their own. The darkness will dull their skin and strip their mind of their reason. It will do nothing to eliminate the memory of their jailer. A sapient being's mind will cling onto anything to keep itself rooted, even a worldview as irrational and poisonous as vengeance.

The moment the chains rust, the prisoner will break out. The resentment they've accumulated over so many years will convert into strength. They will have the power to do anything and everything, and they will not stop until you have suffered just as they have.

So what's the plan?

You take the opposite route. You don't call it confinement, or even house arrest. Those are such horrible-sounding words, aren't they? Let's call it relocation. Re-education. To show how nice you are, you grant the prisoner a decently comfortable room. You feed them three square meals a day. You give them space to walk around. You hire a counsellor and have them sit down and nod their heads and smile placidly as the prisoner clutches their face and weeps out their life story.

It sounds foolish, doesn't it? Wouldn't the prisoner know they're being hoodwinked? At first, they will. The days will drag on. The loneliness will take root. Grant the prisoner a sliver of compassion amidst a sea of isolation, and they will fall upon it like a starving hound to a trail of scraps.

As the days pass, as the prisoner's memories of their old life crumble and are replaced with that small patch of yard with its square view of the sky, the green grass crawling out of the cracks, surrounded by those sturdy walls—that's when you know they've fallen in love with their own chains. Game, set and match.

This method works on the most rambunctious prisoners. For ordinary prisoners, it works so much faster.

Except when it doesn't.

Oh, Ruby. Our hardworking, honest, and constantly bright and peppy Ruby. You remember that time, don't you? This was back in the countryside. You were a growing young lady at the age of twelve and a half. Your appetite had increased. Your thought processes were naturally expanding. You were beginning to look ahead of the morning sun rising above the distant mountains and wondering what lay on the other side.

The head miko didn't like that. Oh no, she did not.

With a flourish of her pen, she doubled your chores. A gesture that demonstrated her fear, but at the time you were too young to understand. The shrine staff told you it was necessary training; your shinme predecessors worked with double your workload. They spoke in gentle tones about how the kami looked favorably on those who worked extra hard to cleanse their parentage's kegare. Young and impressionable and having grown up with horror stories about the traitor named Satono Opal (whose name was forbidden to be spoken by your tongue), you obeyed without hesitation.

You wiped the shrine's floors with that old rag. You recited those prayers under the head miko's watchful eye. You walked up and down the village on errands (but not allowed to run, as an umamusume should). Completing one task led to the beginning of another.

Naturally, the work weighed you down. You became fatigued. Exhausted. But you did not crack, because you wanted to please the people who fed you, clothed you. You sought to prove that you weren't born evil.

Instead, the world cracked you.

Was it heatstroke in summer, or you slipping into the river and almost drowning in winter? Neither. It was nothing so dramatic. You merely closed your eyes, forgot you were walking across the shrine grounds and stumbled over a rock. Your head bashed against the hard ground.

Five minutes. I'm counting them down. Five minutes of your fresh wound bleeding, your frame shaking with the pain and the cold. Five minutes of your mind drifting in and out of consciousness with drool leaking out the side of the mouth, as the shimenawa swayed gently in the breeze. Only then did a priest or a member of a cleaning staff or whoever discover you and escort you to the local hospital.

The diagnosis was straightforward: a concussion. No more shrine work for you. Not even the head miko could go against a doctor's orders.

They bandaged your head. Gave you a checkup. Asked you to read from cards and a long-range eye test in an attempt to reassure normalcy. Too little, too late. Your mind was cracked. A lock was broken instead of being opened with its key. From the keyhole you were unconsciously reaching out, your fingers dipping into a pool as deep as the ocean; as vivid as the colors of the world swirling together; and it showed.

You roamed through your recovery in a daze. Walking felt like controlling puppet strings from afar. Individual grains of rice separated themselves by taste. The cicadas chirped with purpose instead of a single, continuous wail. The visiting shrine priests, who had seemed strict yet fair not a week ago, now sent shivers running up your tail. Whenever the nurse turned off the lights, you would clutch your silver bullet on its chain, and blearily count the writings of the shadows caused by the moon, unaware—yes, unaware, not uncaring—that children were only meant to imagine, not read.

You healed. You returned to the shrine (not home). You resumed your duties, though not with the doubled workload anymore. A few days passed. You were quieter than before. Nobody noticed, nor cared.

That's when the men in the black suits arrived.

They brought the sealed box. They unveiled the contents as your mother's shoes. The head miko brought you to them. She explained that they needed to be burned in a rite of purification to eliminate another cornerstone of Satono Opal's kegare. Only by doing so could the Satono conglomerate move past the scandal that had almost cost them everything in the umamusume racing world and heal.

The head miko thought you were an obedient shinme, since you carried out that double workload of chores without much complaint. She, ironically enough, had begun to trust you like an owner would towards an animal, which meant she overlooked how you couldn't keep your eyes off those shoes. She couldn't see past your blank expression and detect how the fragmented memories of your mother were piecing themselves back together. Her smile, her touch, her strong arms wrapping themselves around you and your sister-cousins in a big hug...each one was as crisp as a freshly printed movie reel. They flashed like sirens. They were painful. You wanted to scream and wail and howl with fresh rage, but the silver bullet told you through its grooves and single notch to keep ears peeled and your mouth shut.

You began to think openly, more deeply. You could not live at the shrine while wearing those shoes. Your legs itched for a proper run. You didn't think you wanted to be a shinme anymore. These thoughts kept mounting inside your little head over and over, an intangible pressure building and building until your restraint snapped like a twig.

You wrote a plan. You tore it up and shoved the scraps in your mouth. Then, you executed.

A few hours before dawn. You tiptoed around your room, throwing what meagre belongings you had in a bag. Spare clothes from the wardrobe. Your rightful allowance from the head miko's office in a cloth purse. You clumsily snipped the wires in the alarm (an outdated motel; the village was not renowned for its technological supremacy) and broke into the back of the shrine's inner sanctum, where you wrapped your mother's shoes around clean paper and shoved them at the bottom of the bag. Footsteps maybe thumped behind you. You weren't taking any chances. You burst out the front door, powered down the stairs and made for the hills.

Across the dirt path, beneath the meagre power lines, the rice paddies fading into the distance—you screamed the entire way. So loud for a young girl, but you deserved it. The shrine were not so cruel to deprive you of running altogether, but they always slammed their heel on the brakes before your body got a good rhythm going. Pent-up anger and sorrow for your mother and sheer instinctual relief all umamusume bathe in during exercise exploded forth in a continuous, unhinged wail.

It was brilliant. It was so cathartic, even for an observer much like yourself. Your eyes, however, were wide with fear.

You were so, so frightened of the audacity of what you were doing. You didn't want to imagine what would happen if you were caught. You knew that hopping on a train at the neighboring village and riding to that mystical land of Tokyo was as safe as wandering into the forest with nothing but the clothes on your back.

Yet, you tried anyway.

That's good. The fact that you've been dreaming this scene repeatedly—that's very good. It means your soul is instinctively responding to the dire straits lurking within Tracen's shadows. You still possess that same unrefined courage. As long as you can muster it alongside the initiative to charge forward and not look back…

…then you'll survive, both in the short-term and the long-term.

My head is turned away, my hands covering my face, yet I perceive your dream as if I were the one at the helm. It's a gross violation of your privacy. Sad to say there are rules even a lonesome umamusume like I am are bound to. Once we meet up in person, I will apologise in person. Things should change, somewhat.

Only a tiny bit further, my lovely Ruby. Your senpai is waiting for you.

"Debate rocks parliament regarding the usage of overhead power lines in urban areas…."

"Scandal or coincidence? The Japanese pop world holds its breath as photos of an UKB48 members are analyzed to see if she was truly entering that Shinjuku hotel with a foreign man…"

"Retired umamusume athlete Toni Bianca has teased a passage from her upcoming autobiography, which centers around her training to win the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe. Pre-orders have skyrocketed in Japan…"

"Painting yourself with white and black stripes wards off pests—a deep dive into the science behind this claim!"

"The Japanese Umamusume Training Academy has reaffirmed their decision to delay the spring try-outs by over a fortnight, citing the recent, inexplicable wave of heavy rainfall damaging both turf and dirt racetracks across the Tokyo region. Umamusume racing fans and members of the URA have expressed concern that students will not have enough time to train themselves before their first maiden race. Director Akikawa has assuaged these concerns via statement saying the academy's landscapers are working hard to restore their internal racetracks back to firm conditions alongside…"

Early Morning, May 13th, 20XX

You gaze out at the turf along with fifty or so other students. It is more mud than grass.

"Oh dear." Grass Wonder says, a hand cupping her cheek. She's next to you. "That is not usable at all."

"We…could practice my running on poor grounds?" You offer.

"That's kind of you to offer, Ruby. I'm afraid this has gone beyond poor and has ventured into the realm of a complete swamp." Grass Wonder lifts her head. Dark clouds rumble on the horizon. A drizzle falls, tiny drops splattering on her and your heads. "I suppose we'll be spending our sessions in the gym for the near future."

You sigh. And here you were looking forward to getting the try-outs done. At least you have more time to think about what kind of race you're running...

3.1: Daily Life III

Mood: Normal.

EXP: 25/140

Afternoon, May 11th, 20XX

The week-only downpour doesn't just coat the academy in a fresh coat of dripping, transparent paint. When thousands of umamusume rely on a certain racetrack to sculpt themselves into the best version they can be for a very prestigious Twinkle Series; and then said racetrack becomes completely unavailable due to flood warnings (that the rest of the city is struck with), those umamusume get heated fast.

"Oi. Oi! Quit swinging those dumbbells in my face!"

"Why don't you get your honor-student ass out of my face, huh?"

"My, my, that's quite an adorable set of puffed cheeks…and flared nostrils you've got there."

"Laugh all you want, Gentil. These chains…are nothing to me!"

"Excuse me. I am sincerely sorry for interrupting you, but you are 9.6 seconds over your allocated time. This, in conjunction with you starting 8.6 seconds late, adds up to a total of 18.2 seconds, which is the average amount of time needed to complete one set of push-ups for the average uma. A single set of push-ups significantly develops the pectoralis major, the triceps brachii and the anterior deltoids—muscles that are crucial to maintaining a smooth rhythm on the turf. One and a half, the rate I can accomplish, more so. Did you know that a moment's hesitation, or rather a lack of it while your opponents suffer from it, can mean the difference between winning and losing in a photo finish? How do you intend to compensate me when I lose due to your tardiness?"

"Flash. Flash! Please calm down. You're scaring the poor girl…"

A mire of fresh sweat and tracksuit odor. A cacophony of metallic squeaks and thrums amidst grunts of exertion. Torsos bump. Faces burn red as tails interlock, and not in the friendly way. This is the state of Tracen's top-of-the-art gymnasium: packed pandemonium not even pop music played over the speakers can pacify.

Behind you—which is near the entrance while in your tracksuit—Hishi Amazon stands guard, belting into a megaphone.

"Listen up, you whelps! The school and I both know you've got important races scheduled and that you're starving for getting as much training done in the wake of the turf flooding. That's why it's extra important that we obey the rules? You hear that? Obey the damn rules. Have your gym tickets printed out or displayed on your phone ready for scanning. Any time wasted fetching those tickets in front of us is going to be cut from your session. We've got no room to be generous. No bargaining or switching up tickets, either. And definitely no trying to sneak past us! Anyone trying to break these rules will be sent straight to Air Groove for a chat with Fuji and my boot up their asses!"

Daitaku Heilos, Tracen's resident gyaru with half a jewelry box's worth of trinkets adorned on her head, storms past you, her normally flapping mouth etched in a tight line. Her footsteps thump like falling meteors amidst the chaos. They snap you out of your daydreaming. Your session starts in less than a minute. Can't waste time here. You take a step…

[Insight check: 9/7 -> Success! +5 EXP.]

"E-everyone's so fired up. They're trying so hard for their races with what limited resources they have…it's a paradise of umamusume effort! We've struck gold today…"

…and promptly turn on your heel to take the long route away. Whoever that girl was, she was definitely another unhinged weirdo. The only unhinged you're willing to deal with today is the state of your musculature as you push it through another grueling training session.

The treadmills are heavily occupied. You mark your name down on the emergency booking list, then decide to pass the time with a nice set of push-ups. You wander over to the designated space area and speak with the umamusume there.

"Excuse me. Could you guys shift to the left a little? I'd like to do my reps here."

These umamusume are not Pelte, Jewel or Tomoe. They remind you of the first day you met the trio, as in the face of your question: they exchange quick glances, one of them smirks, then resume their own reps, as if you hadn't said anything at all.

The beginnings of a frown knead at the sides of your lips. Ah. This again. Isolation—a silent form of harassment. You last saw this back in school over in the countryside. What to do…

Morning, May 16th, 20XX

The constant rainfall finally clears, much to the relief (and still persisting embarrassment) of Japan's weathermen. There's finally an opportunity to run outside without risk of catching a cold. The turf is still out, but the streets and the nearby parks are available. You and Grass Wonder head out in your tracksuit on the first day post-rainfall.

It's a bright, sunny day. The fresh moisture combines with the scent of water-kissed tree leaves to form a lovely refreshment for your lungs. Tiny splashes plop up as your sneakers tread pavement. Your route takes you away from Tracen and around the nearby park, where the once raging river has lapsed into a gentle, if overfilled, stream.

"How's Oguri?" Grass Wonder asks once the two of you cross the bridge.

"You're asking me? Aren't you guys friends?" You reply.

"I wouldn't say we're at that level yet. Acquaintances, more like. Common goals have made us strange bedfellows, though I will say she's a pleasant and insightful uma to chat with. She gave me criticism about my last performance." Grass Wonder says, and there's a hint of an edge to her usual gentle smile. "Are the two of you not talking on LANE?"

"We are." You reply, smiling. It's a point of pride. To think an underground umadol who used to eat leftover burgers from late-night eatery shifts would receive the Ashen Beast's contact details—not that Oguri made a huge fuss about it. She just asked to exchange numbers, and that was that. "She messaged me last night to update me on Kasamatsu."

"The flood relief efforts are still ongoing, then." Grass Wonder comments. "It was such a shock to hear that region hit so hard."

"Yeah. Thankfully, no-one was killed—but there's still a lot of cleanup to go. Houses have collapsed, banks are overflowing, fields are ruined…she's going to be stuck there for a while."

In fact, rumor has it that the moment the first rains increased in intensity, Oguri bolted up from her classroom seat and ran full pelt towards Rudolf's office to ask permission to leave. Even slammed her hands on the Prez's desk like the 'old times'. She and her old Trainer drove straight back home to Kasamatsu, flood warnings be damned. According to a news article you read, the moment Oguri and her Trainer arrived, they got straight to work hauling sandbags, evacuating families, clearing ditches and drains, and all that other messy stuff.

The article was accompanied by a shot of Oguri hauling trucks out of a ditch by pulling them forward, thick ropes stretching across her waist and shoulders. THE HERO OF KASAMATSU RETURNS TO SAVE THE DAY. Inspiring stuff.

It's also the reason why you're not expecting to see Oguri for a while. You understand. Kasamatsu is her family. If a member of FAITHFUL got, say, rescued from a house fire and needed help to recuperate from burns in the hospital, you'd drop your textbooks and exercise plans to rush to visit her too.

Even so, there's something about Oguri that—

"Something bothering you, Ruby?"

You blink. Did your thoughts show on your face? "Nothing!" You chirp.

You instantly know this was the wrong thing to say. Grass Wonder isn't the type of person to squint and stare when she's suspicious. She just asks again.

"Are you sure?"

"It's honestly nothing. I'm probably being silly." You say and chuckle. "C'mon, Grass, you helped me so much on that terrible weekend. It wouldn't be—"

Grass Wonder slows to a halt. She fixes you with a stern look. The unexpectedness of it causes you to stop in your tracks, too.

"Ruby, I mentioned this before, and I'll do it again. I'm your student mentor. It is my job—no, duty—to look after your mental well-being. I'm obviously not as qualified as the academy therapist, but I can lend an ear and talk it out. If something is bothering you, please tell me so we can take care of it.

"But…"

"It's especially crucial that we do, considering the tryouts are due in a few weeks. You don't want to be distracted during training, right?"

You open your mouth to protest, then close it. She's got you there. This thought about Oguri has been niggling at you for the past week and a bit.

Grass Wonder saw you break down in the park, too. She's concerned it might happen again. You're not certain you can tell her the full details about your mother's shoes, since they are so absolutely priceless, but for this one matter she might be of help. You take in a breath and ask, "Is Oguri avoiding me?"

"Didn't you say you talked to her on LANE?"

"Online. In person, it's a bit different. We've only ran across each other a couple of times and it's never enough for a full conversation. I don't want to accuse her anything, but it feels like she's intentionally avoiding some topic. It's kinda awkward."

Grass Wonder blinks. Her ears twitch. Understanding creeps across her face. "I see."

"You know what I'm talking about?" You ask, suddenly alert.

Grass Wonder taps the side of her face. She's thinking about how best to phrase this to you. "Oguri has her own peculiar set of issues to work through." She says.

"They're peculiar?" Another thought occurs to you. "It's not because of me, is it? Gosh, I didn't offend her, did I? Please tell me I didn't."

"No, no, you didn't offend her, but to say her problems are unrelated to you would be grossly incorrect." Grass Wonder says. "She's told me bits and pieces enough for me to make an educated guess on what it's about."

"So—"

Grass Wonder raises her hand. You close your mouth.

"It's just that, however. A guess. Nothing more. It'd feel inappropriate for me to feed you an incomplete story." Grass Wonder clarifies. "I don't want to give you the wrong impression."

It's the right thing to do, you suppose, even if leaves you feeling hollow at being rejected. You nod in silence.

Grass Wonder puts on a gentle smile. "Rest assured, Ruby, Oguri quite likes you. She would never dream of harming you. She's probably just trying to find the right moment.

But what? You ask yourself. That's a question you could dwell on for an entire day and still not come any closer to discerning the truth. Oguri's a surprisingly opaque uma when she wants to be. She loves to eat, she loves to run; both are her obvious joys, but if she doesn't want you to know what lies behind that golden hairband, then by the three goddesses you're not catching a single glimpse of them.

So, you switch tracks.

[Logic check: 72/40 -> Success! +5 EXP.]

Why?

Why is Oguri avoiding you?

Why did Oguri let Grass Wonder know and not you? There's only one reason to hide a truth that's not holding a surprise, and it's guilt.

That short-circuits your thought processes again. You can't fathom what Oguri would ever feel guilty about. She didn't lead you on. She didn't demand your mother's shoes to be finally burned to a crisp. She held you in those strong arms and let you cry until you fell asleep on the spot. If anything, you should feel guilty for not treating Oguri to an all-you-can-eat buffet as thanks!

Is she upset about not stopping you from meeting Diamond? You already told her that wasn't your fault. Back then, you had been stubborn. Had Oguri tried to grab you, you would've yanked free and caught up to Diamond, anyway. You reassured Oguri of these ideas multiple times! What does she have to feel so sorry about? Ugh, this is so confusing!

There's something else: a memory that's brightened in hindsight. The last time you ate lunch with Oguri, she was staring at you over her mountain of fried rice. At the time, you thought it was a trick of the light. You're certain now. Her eyes were misty, and quite sad.

"Tell me this, Grass." You say. "Oguri will tell me about this when she gets back, right?"

"After tryouts. I told her to not interfere with your training. It might break your concentration otherwise."

You could press further but...

[Grass Wonder's Social Link >= 2]

...you do want to trust your friend here.

You sigh. "As long as it happens, eventually."

"I might have allowed it had she not gone back to her hometown, but we both know that wasn't happening in a million years."

"Yeah…"

You'd have called Oguri to ask about this mysterious gripe of hers, but that damned downpour. No chance in hell you're interrupting her rescue work for your personal troubles. It's already a miracle she's found space to exchange greetings on LANE.

With a brief exchange of nods, you and Grass Wonder resume jogging through the city.

Half-way through, one of Grass Wonder's friends stumbles across the pair of you and offers to help you train. It is…

Morning, May 18th, 20XX

A vending machine rests at the base of the Three Goddesses' statue.

By itself, the vending machine is not unusual. They're products of Tracen's sponsorship deals with sporting and athletic companies. Most vending machines produce healthy snacks and drinks for the students to enjoy: sparkling water, protein balls, cooled carrot sticks and so on. The one in the cafeteria that serves chocolate and chips tends to break down half the time, for whatever reason, but it's the sole anomaly. The prices are reasonable, and the goods are delivered fast. No, you find yourself thinking, you don't have a problem with this new vending machine by itself.

The placement, however, draws a grimace. Putting a symbol of corporate convenience near the base of Tracen's most prominent cornerstone of faith reeks of impropriety, even to a former shinme. It should've been put on one of the paths leading away from this section of the school grounds. That's how the larger city shrines allocate their vending machines: in the outer rim of the shrine.

"Anshinzawa's Extremely Amazing and Ultra-Genius Health Supplements?" You read out the sign aloud. "Guaranteed to activate your chakras?"

The front of this new vending machine is plastered with a colorful depiction of a middle-aged human woman with long blonde hair, curvy sunglasses atop a sharp nose, and a string of large pearls around her neck. She's dressed in a tight-fitting red dress with a white lab coat on top. This…

[Artistry check: 54/50 -> Success! +10 EXP.]

...reminds you of a fashion trend from before you were born. It was from the bubble era of the late 1980s, a time of unprecedented economic prosperity for the nation as a result of massive trends in the real estate stock market. Madame Sugar belonged to that era. She loved telling FAITHFUL stories about the time she worked as a set dresser and hostess for some of the best cabaret clubs Shinjuku and Kabukicho had to offer. Her old photos were displayed in frames around her shop. The girls in them were striking: Tight, short-fitting dresses in shiny metallic fabrics, colorful sequins and heavy accessories. Lot of lip gloss and eyeshadow to go around.

There were movies in that bubble era, too. Manager Suzuki, in a surprise twist, recommended his favorites. The men were slick, the girls were bombshells, and the cars tore up the highway. You remembered thinking that era must have been fun, in a chaotic, messy way. Too bad some politician invented a special tax that ended up pricking the whole thing.

Therefore, this Anshin person…is in her fifties or sixties? The proportions are there. Yep, sounds about right. That smile, though. It's too flashy. You don't trust it. Why is she making the peace sign, too?

"You found it too, huh?"

A voice from behind. You whirl around, guard up. An uma wearing a grey beanie stands a short distance away, one hand on her hip. You lock eyes, and she approaches, showing the length of brown hair from behind her boyish cut at the front.

The way her tail sways and her hips move is casual, almost languid, yet your own ears stiffen in exchange. Your fingers twitch for the silver bullet. This girl approached you with purpose. She is not another face in the crowd.

"Have we met?" You ask.

"Nah." The girl says. She sucks on a lollipop, the act slightly slurring her words. "But I've heard of you."

"I see." You say, cautiously. "Is this the part where you call my mother a whore and ask me to neck myself?"

The girl blinks. Her eyes go slightly wide—for a second. Then she's back to normal. "Nah. I couldn't care less about your mom's reputation." She says, shrugging. "It's in the past. We're in the present, and so is this baby of a machine."

She gives the vending machine a tap on the side. The metallic frame rattles. She leans on it.

"Let tell you a story." The girl says. "You heard of mutton ice-cream?"

"Mutton? As in the meat that comes from a sheep?" That's savory. Ice-cream is sweet. The clash of the two twists your features with disgust. The girl barks out a peal of laughter.

"Yep, that's the one. It wasn't ordinary mutton, though. It was grilled mutton, the type they serve in actual restaurants, and it used to be sold in the school store for a bit. Sales weren't great. They soon dropped to zero. Word began to spread that the ice-cream was cursed."

"Can't imagine why." You say, sarcasm dripping like the drizzle from last week.

"Yeah, who doesn't love all that salt and meat rolling over their tongue for the day? People, right? But, y'know, rumors started brewing. They said that eating the ice-cream brought you bad luck. Forgetting answers on quizzes, setting their tail on fire, dropping their shoes out the window…that kind of stuff."

You fold your arms. "You ate it, right?"

She grins.

"Got it in one. Me, my cousin and this new girl we picked up along the way."

Her grin stretches, and now it feels slightly cocky. There's a hint of playfulness in her words as well. The type you get when you know something the other doesn't.

"So, what do you think happened next?"

You pause, deliberately so. "You guys threw up into the toilet?"

"Nah."

"You tripped down the stairs and broke your carrots in three?"

"Nope."

"You spent all week doing gate tests only to be distracted by the last second by some random in the stands and ended up losing an entire second behind the rest of the competition?"

The girl whistles. "You've got some imagination, Miss Enka. Still frigid as crap, though."

You roll your eyes. "I don't know."

The girl snickers. She leaves you hanging for a few seconds, during which you stare blankly at her, then answers.

"Nothing."

"Nothing?" You repeat.

"Yup. Absolutely nothing. The curses weren't real. We ate the ice-cream and didn't feel a damn thing besides it tasting like puke." The girl takes a long, hard suck of her lollipop, then pulls it out, twirling by her hands, as you boggle at her. "Fun, isn't it?"

Your hands fall by your side. You count to ten, hope reality shifts…nope, it's still there.

"W-what the heck does this have to do with this gaudy-looking vending machine?" You bluster, feeling and only barely resisting the urge to slap yourself in the face until your forehead cracks from the impact. Ebisu, I swear—

"Absolutely nothing at all." The girl sings. "All those rumors were made up. Anyway, this local acupuncturist of ours was inspired by that ice-cream story of ours—thought it meant curses didn't exist—so she began peddling her wares in front of the school statue."

She strides up to the vending machine. A callused finger runs over the rim of the thin coin slot. "I gotta say though, this one might be cursed for real."

You can't help but ask, if only because you're experiencing whatever the conversation equivalent of the sunk-cost fallacy is.

"Why?"

"Because this acupuncturist worked on that same cousin of mine. Gave her that strength 'chakra'. Turned her into a roaring monster on the track. Won her a G1. The other girls she worked on? Complete failure. They stumbled out of the building like zombies. It's a roll of the dice with that woman."

A chill runs down your spine. The suspicion you projected onto this girl has transformed into tension. It's cold and heavy, yet sharp in its intensity. It's reminiscent of the times you tried picking out coffin motels before Saya gave you the run-down; a spin of the silver bullet, a prayer to the heavens. Faith put entirely on whimsical, cruel luck.

[(World Resonance check: 70/50) || (Insight check: 10/9) -> Success! +10 EXP.]

And the uma before you revels in that faith. She loves dangling her toes above the razor's edge. She has surely held the racing equivalent of a revolver with five chambers loaded to the side of her head.

The hoodie'd girl extends her right hand. She stretches her palm, flexes her fingers. She pulls back her arm and slams it straight onto the vending machine's buttons, not bothering to give any label a single glance.

At the fringes of what you can see, almost hidden by her long brown locks, you witness a maniacal, almost-feral smirk, accompanied by one eye gazing back at yours. That ferocity has enveloped you before, you realise, and it was from the courtesy of one Meisho Tabaru.

Oh. So that's who her cousin is...

The vending machine hums. It spits out a single can. The girl withdraws it from the bottom and takes a deep chug.

"Delish." She says, licking her lips. "Tastes like the rainwater back home."

Afternoon, May 21st, 20XX

A tap on your shoulder. You turn around, an armful of books cradled against your chest.

"You're still here."

It's Narita Brian. Blunt cut, rope in her hair, a stalk chewing in her mouth. Her stance firm, her expression as stony as the day you met.

Once more, she invades your space, closing the distance in a stride and staring down at you. Nose tilted up, eyes scanning your face. It is arrogance and pure self-assurance and it is formidable.

A month ago, you crumpled in front of this mighty Triple Crown winner. This afternoon, you straighten yourself, relax your arms and look straight back at her.

This time, you stand your ground.

[Composure check: 60/50 -> Success! +10 EXP.]

"Yep, I still am. I'm a proper Tracen student." You reply and offer Narita Brian a smile. "How may I help you?"

Her eyebrows slightly raise. She grunts through a chew of her stalk, then steps back. That might have been a sign of approval. You'll take it.

"How's your trainer? Is she still sick?" You ask.

Narita Brian scoffs. "As if a bout of pneumonia could ever keep that woman down. You're not busy, right?"

"Nope. Just got out of the library."

"Good. I need an extra pair of eyes. Follow me."

She drags you to the student council room, an office-like space with individual desks, long tables arranged in a rectangular U-shape, and a whiteboard littered in diagrams and scribbles. Textbooks are stacked on a shelf. A kettle and several clean mugs are arranged in a neat row on a table adjacent to a wall of framed certificates. Gentle sunlight from the sole window casts a soft, orange glow across the furniture.

You initially panic at the prospect of meeting Rudolf again, tail swishing back and forth as your brain tries to put together your PR lessons into an introduction worth speaking, but the student council president is not here. The room is deserted.

"What's this about?" You ask.

Narita Brian walks over to one of the desks and opens it. She dumps the machine onto the spot near you. You peer at the screen and see...photos of flowers?

"Air Groove's having a hard time deciding what flowers to switch out on display at the reception and a bunch of other rooms this fortnight, mostly because she's busy as hell with other duties." Narita Brian says. She eyeballs you. "You worked as an umadol, right?"

Her tone is flat. You can't decide if she approves of your past career or not.

"Yes?" You reply, hesitantly?

"You guys deal with flower motifs before?"

"Also yes?" As part of the training, though it wasn't exactly the group's main focus…

"Better than two of the other girls I grabbed. We can use your outside opinion, then. Work together with her and figure this out." Narita Brian says, pointing to another student who has just walked in through the door.

Her happens to be one of your fellow rookies, one who is talked about with praise by the staff and the Trainers at that…

Early Morning, May 27th, 20XX

[World Resonance: 70/70 -> Success! +10 EXP.]

You're out running on Tracen grounds on your usual early morning jog, mind wandering amidst the feel of your body, when you hear it: a muffled scream. Shocked, you divert course and arrive at a particular tree stump. It's the Tracen Stump, the place where umas go to scream out their frustrations at losing.

There's someone bent over there, their head fully immersed in the center of the trunk. Dawn has only just crept past the horizon. As a result, you can't make out a single feature of this uma's face.

"Are you alright?" You ask, crouching down next to her.

The wind whistles. A cool breeze, brushing past your hair. Goosebumps bristle. It's a cool morning today.

"I'm tired." The girl says. Her voice is muffled.

"I'm sorry to hear that." You reply.

The girl doesn't move from her spot. You can feel her sneer from inside the trunk's dark confines.

"Are you? Are you really?" The girl demands.

"Yes. Yes, I am. I'm sorry that you're hurting." You say. "I can't help you turn back the clock, nor magically cure your tiredness, but I do know what it's like to be exhausted on your feet."

"Exhausted." The girl repeats. Her fingers tighten around the stump's edge. "That's a funny word. It's exactly what I am."

"It's tough, isn't it?"

"That's what they all say." The girl grouses. "Be grateful to enter Tracen. Take the most of these opportunities. You're already better than most of the regional stock."

That last one is an objective truth, one you wore with pride when you received your acceptance letter. The uma in front of you is far from pleased.

"To hell with it all!" She shrieks. "I'm tired of being told those platitudes. I'm tired of training, tired of waking up early in the morning, tired of listening to bullshit commands from stupid Trainers with their heads not screwed on tight and I'm tired, exhausted, sick to the bones and just so goddesses damned done with losing all my races!"

Her ranting ascends into a full-blow howl that seems to vibrate the very ground itself. Her fingers dig into the wood so hard they threaten to splinter the foundation of the stump itself. You instinctively take a step back, feeling the hair on the back of your neck rise.

"I'm nothing…" The girl moans brokenly. "My legs don't work. I wanted to be hopeful and beautiful and spirited and determined and now nothing…"

You reach forward, ready to offer the girl a pat on the shoulder. You stop, right above making contact, as the girl speaks again.

"Satono Ruby. I know who you are."

You smile, weakly. "Who doesn't?"

"I've seen you prance around the school."

"Not the word I'd use."

"You disgust me." The girl hisses.

"That's…also not new, I suppose."

If the girl were standing, she'd be glaring at you, and her cheeks would be purple. Somehow, you know this to be fact.

"Your mother abandoned you. Your own family despises you. Most of the school giggles and sneers behind your back. Just yesterday they tried dumping your homework down the gutter. You should have stolen a knife and stabbed some pedestrian long ago, or at the least landed yourself in juvie. Instead, you're at Tracen. Tracen! The best racing academy in the nation! How can you stand there and take everything you have been dealt with a smile?" The girl wails. "Answer me!"
