Late Morning, July 2nd, 20XX

At first, you attempt to seal your misshapen childhood in the mental chest where it belongs. The more time you spend kvetching about yourself, the later you can get back to what actually matters in your life. It's difficult, sadly enough, to blank your mind when the muscle memory slips onto your hands like a favorite pair of gloves the moment you hold the broom.

The shrine is the Tokyo Racetrack; you tell yourself, in hushed, strained mental tones. The broom in your hand is not wood but…a ceremonial weapon, painted in aerosol and constructed from hollow aluminum. It's the spear of the ronin in disguise, a matching piece to the nagitana Grass posed for with that magazine shoot. The silver bullet beading against your heating skin is also part of this mysterious G1 outfit, since Kaori has lost brain cells and let you keep it instead of rescinding it for being a choking hazard. And your bodily motions in-flight are of…the janitors cleaning up the clumps of dirt and grass from the umas tearing up the track.

[Artistry check: 58/100 -> Failure.]

You heave a sigh. Nope. You can't keep pretending. Sweeping and scrubbing in a shrine atop a mountain? That's a task as unsexy as a pile of dirt, as divorced from the thrill of the race as Pluto is from the Sun.

"Something wrong, Ruby?"

You answer Machan. It's an almost instant manoeuvre—you anticipated her breath from behind. "Thinking of you."

She blinks. She halts her sweeping, then scratches the side of her cheek. "Um…"

"Umadol tactic. That's an umadol tactic. Saying the line and shooting through the heart." You say out, "I did it to my supporters at handshake events, with the heart-sign and the handsigns and in my kimono and crap."

"Alright," Machan states. "And what's actually going on?"

"I'm having brain signals that are firing off 'uggh' and 'why me' and I'm tempted to hurl a fragile object at a hard surface." You reply. Machan doesn't flinch. One perk of hanging around Aston Machan is the ability to say as ludicrous and inane a topic, as common sense will allow, and she'll smile and nod gently and guide you through those thought processes.

"This is boring." You begin, resuming with your broom.

"Mm-hm," Machan hums.

"Soooo boring."

"Totally."

"And I was thinking. Thinking that if I ditched you here and now to run off and go train my glutes or something, I'd feel awful about myself. But I'd score another minor win for my debut, which is urgent and pressing, but again I'd have blown you off, which means I'd feel more terrible and I couldn't enjoy the celebratory cake." You flick your hand. "You get that feeling?"

"Not the first time one of my good friends tried to play hooky. You should've seen how Vodka used to act on her first day. She practically vibrated through her seat. Then, she met Daiwa Scarlet, and well, the rest is history. You're more diligent than she was. You're still here."

"Griping and moaning…"

"I mean, I'm tempted to ditch math class. It's not that uncommon."

"Not for me. This is a first." You mutter. Mostly because it was never an option. The shrine was inescapable, and missing out on shifts in Shibuya came with the risk of getting fired. You then had to grind to tail off to pass Tracen's entrance exams. It's been months of soft beds and free meals with extra time to spare and—oh goddesses, has your time at Tracen softened you up? You totally would've cleaned a shrine or two in exchange for 'work experience' and a free lunch back last year, wouldn't you?

"Somehow, I bore myself to tears in lit, yet I tuck my legs in like a good little uma and stay put. Not here. Not the Tracen-mandated official shrine." You grumble.

"Do you hate brooms, Ruby? You sound like it. In any case, I'd say playing hooky is unnecessary, seeing as, well…" Machan sweeps her gaze left and right, her short ponytail lagging behind. "You're almost done!"

She sound astonished. As if to emphasize, she shoves a finger out, her eyes widened. Through your mulling and the brief conversation, you've tidied up the courtyard. You swept the leaves, pulled out the weeds, took out the trash down to the hillside path near the mountainside street, then swept up a smattering of loose gravel. The courtyard has transformed from a messy, pockmarked garbage dump into a slab of pure, pristine concrete goodness, all thanks to you.

She gestures to the scene in front of you. Machan echoes the sentiment. She sounds awestruck. "Great job!"

Strains under your arms, sweat beading on your forehead, these are scraps of evidence that speak of powering through the backlog like a fleshy machine. Yet, all you can think is that it's not a complete job. Merely a tick on the long list of defects you've spotted. The damaged rafter, the dead wasp nests that could be reused, the flecks of rust speckled across the wind chimes and the meager offerings…

You scowl.

This is inexcusable. These thoughts—they are execrable. Look. Look, damn it! Past the fence, down the hill: the city skyline is right there. Fuchu City, citadel of concrete towers and metallic spires, of modernity, consumerism and URA glory. Forget the countryside, Satono Ruby, because this land has long surpassed that epoch, and you, standing atop his hill in the present moment, are no longer a miko, but a product of said modernity. An aspirant of the Twinkle Series, determined to blaze your own trail of glory through its storied history. So what if Tracen and the Association of Shinto Shrines forced you here? They drew up an agreement. They defined the beginning and end of your involvement in fine print. You'll do what is required, leave the rest, like that moldy water basin, and you'll relish it.

Look, you are packing away the brooms and buckets right now!

The door slams shut behind you as you stalk off. Machan trails behind, presumably still smiling.

You're about to storm up to the groundskeeper and loudly demand your next task, when you notice him occupied. He's sitting on the steps of the shrine's interior building, fiddling with sheets of white paper. He's folding them. As mad as you are, you're not about to interrupt someone when they're busy.

"Zig-zags," Machan remarks, dropping her voice. "He's folding them like origami."

"They're shide." You answer automatically.

"Pardon?"

"Never seen them at shrines during New Year's? They're…" Is it too late to retract? No. Not when you've already given an answer. "They're strips of paper that ward off bad evil and impurities."

"Ooh, like Matikanefukukitaru's deal. Her tags are more ornate and inky in that traditional occult fashion."

From a distance, it's a serene sight: an old man existing in repose, brushed by a gentle breeze and basking in warm sunlight.

Machan frowns. "He seems to be struggling."

She's correct. The more you examine the groundskeeper, the more you realise this is no tranquil scene. This is you peering from afar at a old man's lack of finesse. The groundskeeper's hands shake as he works. His knobby old fingers twist and bend the papers at odd angles, and he can't align the scissors right. For every one page he presses into a successful pattern, he fails with another. It's a waste of time and effort.

"Are you alright, sir?" Machan calls.

The groundskeeper looks up. For an instant, you see his tired frown. He brightens up the moment he catches sight of you, then hobbles over to check on the courtyard.

"Well done. Very well done, both of you!" The groundskeeper exclaims. "I've never seen this courtyard so clean."

"It was mostly Ruby here." Machan says, nudging you on the shoulder. "She's the expert. I was merely her assistant."

"Oh, don't be so modest. I'm sure you performed an excellent job, too." The groundskeeper chirps. "Just a wipe-down of the furniture inside and you're off home."

[Orphaned: Exists.]

You squint at him. "Wait, that's it?"

"Very much sure. Nothing else." The groundskeeper says.

"Are you sure?" You persist.

The groundskeeper's grin falters. "Don't got more work for you, and you must be busy, so…"

No, no, this doesn't sound right.

You know how these old folks operate. They either forget important details, or pretend they've forgotten so they can spring on the young help later as a test. The head miko was one example. That crappy manager at Uma Fried Chicken, under whom you slaved for a couple of months for food money, was as well. The bastard kept giving you last-minute tasks because you were young and naïve, or so he thought.

Now, this groundskeeper. Is he going to stand there, misshapen paper in hand, and pretend your duties end with sweeping, organizing, wiping stuff down and taking out the trash? You don't mind more. It's covered in the contract and all. You'd wish he'd be more honest about it. You caught him fumbling with those papers, for crying out loud!

"Absolutely, absolutely, sure?"

Machan elbows you in the stomach, earning you a sharp cough and a sudden jerking of your head back. "Apologies, sir." She says, "My friend here aims to be conscientious in her day-to-day activities. She likes to keep her room spick and span."

It's not a lie. You've invited Machan over to bust your brains at troublesome maths problems. Tidying up your living space was a habit developed from street life; a single possession lost meant the difference between eating and starving.

"She might have…" Machan grins cheekily, "Had a mental switch flipped at seeing the mess."

You stare at Machan, scandalized. She winks back. The groundskeeper forms another grin. "Work ethic. Always pleasant to see it on you young'uns. You're Tracen girls—that goes without saying. Apologies."

"Oh, Ruby here is a very hard worker. She'd earn the fastest learner award half a dozen times over if it existed. As for me? I'm not bad myself."

Machan giggles like those grannies you've noticed hanging around those old-timey shopping lanes. The groundskeeper chuckles in turn.

"We've basically allocated ourselves an early break. Not to pile too much on our shoulders, since you said we were busy girls, but we will be here for a moment longer, so if there's anything else…"

The groundskeeper shoves his hand up. "No more work."

"Sir?"

"You've all done enough. You all have lives to return to. Enjoy them."

He describes to you the finer details of the wipe-down, of which there aren't many. The wipe-down is the end, as mentioned earlier. Equipment's inside near the kitchen; you're welcome to look around, but please do not poke your noses in the cupboards or the fridge. His medication lives in there. The drop, the last-minute surprise, what have you, never arrives. The groundskeeper waves a hand and returns to fumbling with his half-formed shides.

Creating a shide is not as easy as folding a zig-zag pattern from a piece of paper. You need to cut strips into the thin papers at equal segments, then fold those newly made flaps around and around until an overarching, overlaid zig-zag pattern is formed. It doesn't end at one shide, either. You're meant to hang them up in multiple places: the rafters, indoors, along trees. The more shide placed, the more kegare is warded off, after all. Beyond that, spares must be made. Washi paper is durable, but paper is by nature soft and prone to shriveling up into messy clumps during autumn rains.

The task is easy enough if you've practiced and your hands are nimble. The groundskeeper's pair have long since brushed past the expiration date. Yet, he persists, refusing to ask the two umas with healthy hands behind him. He'll sit there in the sun for an hour or more, the back of his neck baking, with a single small bottle of water to quench of thirst.

You enter the shrine's interior. You mix soap and warm water and dunk a sponge in the middle, wooden-faced. The furniture squeaks beneath your frantic scrubbing. Your mind tries to blank itself, yet your muse, that traitorous woman, refuses to stay deaf. She weaves a tune, set to the melody of discarded FAITHFUL drafts and playlists from a run-down transistor radio you once owned. Look at him, Ruby, the chords sneer. Look at his trembling back, then what's beyond that. The curvature of his hunch on his seat, enough for apples to roll off. His skin is a rice bag of leathery white and flecks of desert sand, and his straw hat is poked with tiny holes for crows; they match in a uniform of poverty. Walk up to him, and you are sure to hear his ragged wheezing, in and out, half and half, the nutrients in the air unable to filter through his weary lungs. Isn't it pathetic? Isn't it ridiculous and pathetic, this man dedicating the twilight of his years in devotion to the shrine, the kami, who will never thank him, not to mention the teenage uma who entered his home, griping and internally moaning within his hospitality whilst comparing him to the coldest, worst elderly woman she's ever met.

And she's doing that, not because he's berated her—he hasn't. Not because he's ordered to kneel and recite prayers—he also hasn't done that. Nor has he called her mother a filthy kegare-stained mistake. No, that teenage uma is comparing and sizing them both up, because that man and that woman are in charge of shrines. That's it! Seriously, what a stretch! They can't find mental gymnastics that brilliant at the chess Olympics. Honestly, what in the name of Saint Lite is that uma thinking?

Welp, good thing you're not her, right?

Right?

Your stomach twists.

Arthritis. The term pops into your head as you scrub a stubborn stain off the floor. You watched a clip from some Umatok doctor; the moving diagrams of the bones grinding and wearing themselves down, through no cause but usage alone, horrified you as an aspiring athlete. It's happening to the man right as you work. How long does he have left? A year? Two years? Five, at most? You're no rheumatologist.

"Machan, you've worked with the elderly, yeah?"

"Why do you ask?"

You jerk a thumb behind you. "Is that guy receiving good care?"

"Are you concerned about him?"

"I mean…" You stammer. "Who wouldn't? Out of passing interest, that is. Prior to today, I've never seen him in my life."

Machan pauses. Rag drooping in hand, she regards you. There's a discerning, almost hypnotic quality to the look from beneath her usual demureness. It's enough to make you squirm. She ultimately shakes her head. "He wouldn't be here, nor would this shrine exist in its current state, if he were."

"This is Japan, not America. Health care is sort of okay here!"

Machan gives you a sympathetic look. "My mom's a doctor, Ruby. One of the hard facts of her profession is that you can't force someone to receive care if they don't want to."

You tear your gaze away from your friend. Damn it, you think. Damn Machan for giving the blinding, obvious answer. Damn the groundskeeper for existing in his situation.

Imaginary Kaede, Hotaru, Manager Suzuki, Grass, Kaori—stop. Close those mouths. You understand. You understand, damn it. Him in your shoes, the golden rule, objective reality, you understand it all, damn it. You're going. Again, please shut up.

You stomp out of the shrine's interior. Machan calls after you; you don't answer. It's as if your legs move by themselves. Before you finish blinking, you're behind the old man, your long shadow overlapping his hunched-over form.

The old man glances up..

"How may I help you, young lady?"

"Those shide…"

"Oh! You recognise the name."

"Read it in a book. Took origami classes, whatever. I'll help you."

The old man blinks. He raises a hand again. "Like I said, I don't need it—"

"Yeah, well, I disagree." You drop onto the wooden stairs beside him, take an empty shade of paper, twisting your fingers and wrists in a what should be a flurry of miracles to his wizened gaze, and produce a competent shide.

The groundskeeper holds it up to the sunlight, his jaw open. "It's perfect. You're good, young miss!"

"I'm an expert." You mumble back. Because the head miko would jab the underside of your chin with her ofuda if you produced a single error.

The groundskeeper tries to prise the papers out of his hand, his expression etched in concern. You're too swift. You grab the stack and fold through the shade. Machan drops by and sits down. When you tell her to leave, she says it wouldn't be 'cash money' of her to abandon her good friend to play by herself. It's a Vodka phrase, apparently.

Machan ends up a natural, thanks to her expertise in folding paper cranes for the other patients. You expected as much, after learning about her hospital childhood. The rest of the shide are done and folded in minutes.

You're not done. There's a fervor rising in your belly, half-spiteful, half thrilling. Cracking your knuckles, you drag Machan and the groundskeeper for a second tour of the shrine. You point out the rafter damage. You grab the broom back and whack down the dead wasp nests, then spray special perfume to ward off the rest. You take a hammer and nails and patch up holes in the support beams. Next is calling the old repairman who always fixed the Anafabula offices for his extensive handyman network. He tosses you a number of a team with decent rates and a fair warranty.

Machan jots notes. She pulls out her mini-recorder and speaks into it.

You go inside, replace the wax in the inside laterns and recycle what's available. You push painted plastic into the statues' gaps to conceal them until the repairs arrive.

"You're a miracle worker, young missus! Did you volunteer on behalf of the Association before?" The groundskeeper has a twinkle in his eyes now. He looks at you as if you're his long-lost granddaughter.

Oh, so now he's happy to receive your help?

"Sorta. Countryside."

"Which one?"

"Osaka." It's a lie.

"Would you consider a next time?"

In your dreams—

Not a snowball's—

Go to—

"If the Prez asks of me."

You resume shoving grey plastic putty into the front statues' gaps to conceal the damage until the real repairment arrive. That's it. That's the last of what you can sufficiently do, and it's cost you an hour and a half of your life that you'll never get back.

You catch Machan. She's smiling wider, and there's a warmth in her eyes.

The old man heads into his private quarters and returns with a tin of ginger candies, mumbling about how he'd be so rude to let you and Machan go without a reward. They're the expensive kind, you notice, created from a date in the past fifty years. A dead ringer for the head miko's own snacks. Together, you and Machan bow and thank the groundskeeper. Then you flee down the stairs, head to the karaoke den and scream your lungs hoarse.

"Standing at the tip of my imagination, I laughed and told 'em I wouldn't come back. That trembling voice in my head, my warrior shivers said!"

The walls of the karaoke vibrate with joy. Shared joy. They're a gaudy shade of pink and purple with gold diamonds arranged in patterns, which speaks of richness and bounty, and these are all good auras that you are resonating and brimming with right now!

"Ruby."

"What is it, my fantastic friend Aston Machan?" You shout back, twisting your neck away from the karaoke screen.

Machan catches a glimpse of you through the strobing ceiling lights. She winces. It's a gentle scrunch of her face, rather than the hard, line-forming cringe found in Tosen Jordan. In any other time, you'd find it harrowing. Now, it's hilarious. "I hate to bring this topic up, but are you okay?"

"Peachy. One hundred percent peachy! Because today! I did it."

"Did what?" Machan asks.

"I did it!" You holler.

"Elaborate, Ruby!" Machan hollers back over the guitar shredding.

You belt a peal of laughter. "I helped that old grandpa, Machan. I tore my ex-miko skills out of my head-shoebox and cleaned up that shrine lickety-split. I made his day, gave him a real excuse to go down to the city and see his grandchildren, and it was all because of me and you, we're the champions today, Machan, and we did it all while I was seeing the shadow of the worst woman I've ever met! She was an absolute cunt, Machan!"

Bad Ruby. Very bad Ruby, spewing out an actual swear. Machan recoils, all pretense gone. The song reaches it crescendo, the handsome guitarist shredding our chords, and your voice reaches a fever pitch.

"Slap me with an award. Take me to the Bukodan. Tell Secratriat to go to hell, because I'm the most amazing uma to ever live!"

Fireworks explode in a bloody cherry-red fracas. You strike a pose, finger shot up rigid towards the heavens.

Machan sits in her seat, unimpressed. She is a sensible girl who has retained her sanity. She patiently waits for you to burn out and collapse on the seats before scooting over.

"Want to talk about it?"

You sip your complimentary orange juice, glum, your knees tucked together. In your fever, you hurled the microphone against the wall. "Maybe."

It has struck you that you just blurted out a non-insubstantial amount of your history in this small space to one of the more observant, silently inquisitive members of your generation. It's lucky Machan is such a nice girl to hang around and not, say, a paparazzo, because if your childhood was leaked to the press, you might as well crawl under a rock and stay there for the rest of your life.

"Now, I'm no psychologist." Machan begins.

"No, you're not. You're better than those frauds." You mutter out.

"I did listen to my mother's patients in her clinic as they recuperated. And I have mediated between what feels like an old married couple. I'd say I know a couple of things." Machan says. She takes your hand and traces a gentle line across the back of it. "Let's begin?"

You take a shuddering breath. Your head is clear, past the weariness. "Okay."

"Would you describe today as a waste of time?"

(Was today a waste of time? Choose only 1.)

[] [DailyLife3Part1] Yes, because I had to work for free.

[] [DailyLife3Part1] Yes, because the shrine should never have gotten to such a poor condition in the first place.

[] [DailyLife3Part1] Yes, because now I have less time to do what I want.

[] [DailyLife3Part1] No, because I helped the groundskeeper and did a good thing.

[] [DailyLife3Part1] No, because Machan was there.

[] [DailyLife3Part1] No, because I got fresh air and sunshine.

[] [DailyLife3Part1] Yes, No, Maybe? It shouldn't have gotten that bad and I'm glad to help, but it needs a more permanent solution

[] [DailyLife3Part1] Write-in.

(Apologise for swearing? Choose only 1)

[] [DailyLife3Part2] Apologise for swearing.

[] [DailyLife3Part2] Do not apologise for swearing.

Night, July 3rd, 20XX

"I don't think it's much of a mystery whom that residue belongs to."

"Don't be rude, senpai! You don't know that. It could be some other coffee enjoyer."

The amount of disdain radiating Plain Jane could power Tracen's greenhouses for months. "Please be rational with me here, Ruby. There is no other uma in this academy as fanatical about coffee as Miss Manhattan Cafe."

And you think fanatical is such a crude word. It might be the basis of 'fan', but fans don't pull out torches and pitchforks over the slightest subversion from the norm (much). Manhattan Cafe isn't a uma who'd grow enraged over her friends or Trainer forgoing her brews for a quick Umabucks iced tea, or whatever. It's so rude to think poorly of your fellow Tracen girls when they're not acting like unhinged weirdos.

Sadly, you don't get a chance to dump this argument because Plain Jane pushes you on the shoulders with the flat of her hands, sending you soaring through an arc that lands you in her paddock lake. You plunge through the freezing cold water and wake up back in your bed. It's in the middle of the night, so you fall asleep immediately.

Morning arrives. Teeth brushed, morning exercise complete, homework only half-ignored, you gulp down breakfast and endure the boring morning classes. The morning recess bell rings. You dump your books on the back shelf and leave the classroom with gusto.

[World Resonance check: 108/40 -> Success! Trivial: +0 EXP.]

The phenomena are exactly where they were last time: plastered across the section of floor in front of the library door, an inky black, squirming, writhing doormat. The surface shimmers in the iridescent swirls of an oil spill. The shape speaks of a monster straight out of an old tome, yet umas mill to and fro, their slip-ons stepping into the mire and exiting with no physical trace.

You crouch down next to it, pretending to have dropped a pen, and twitch your nose. It smells fresh. A newly brewed cappuccino, with a hint of dark chocolate, if that bitter-sweet scent is to be believed. The trails appearing so vivid and the scent so strong is a sure sign that the owner, Manhattan Cafe, is near. Probably. You hope. It's like bloodstains in detective movies. The older the trail, the further away the target, and vice-versa.

You stand up. You grab the library door handle and swing it open. Today is the day you track down Manhattan Cafe, treat her to a melon bread or something, and determine if she has any relation to magic or the Nightmare. The specifics of your introduction elude you. You don't care. That's the fun part of socializing: falling back on basic conversational tricks and going with the flow! And you'll be right while Plain Jane is wrong. That's also quite important.

You smirk. This is going to be so easy.

[Sneak check: 56/100 -> Failure.]

Two days later, you limp down another section of hallway, head hung and with the discovery that, no, it was not easy. It was failure. Total utter failure. So wide an emotional chasm tearing at your heart, you wish you could tear your crown ornament off your head and bulldoze the entire library with the force of your throw.

Manhattan Cafe was not in the library, despite the presence of the creeping shadows. She was not lurking at the end of a hallway you dashed down, ducking and weaving through the crowd. She was not in the academy cafeteria, the changing rooms, the bicycle rack belonging to the gym, an empty classroom, or the academy store where her sponsored coffee beans are sold! But you tore through those areas like a mad dog with raw steak up its nostrils, anyway! Now the spectacled librarian, the gym manager, the head lunchlady, and countless other Tracen students must think you're some pushy busybody who sticks her nose in places where it doesn't belong.

Are you going insane? Like, who else in this academy radiates coffee scent from her soul? You dare not approach Plain Jane in Soul Form at night; you can visualize her smug grin in her head. And then, oh goodness, she'll pat your head and say you did your best and—argh!

Enough is enough. You refuse to beat a dead ox. A change of tactics is required: if you can't find Manhattan Cafe by yourself, you'll go to someone who can!

That's why you're standing patiently outside a specific Trainer's Room in the middle of the academy, waiting for the door to slide open.

"Watcha doing here, kiddo?"

A punk trapped in a maid's dress. The spikes are as sharp and shiny as ever. It's Maid Black, or to use her proper name, Trainer Shion, wearing her disinterest on her sleeves. Her teeth chew through a red jelly bean.

"Come for scrim with Rice, have you?" She asks. "No can do, I'm afraid. She's out with Hiromi on the track today."

"No, I'm for your other trainee." You reply.

She cocks an eyebrow. "Cafe? What about her?"

"I'm kinda searching for her." You reply.

"Why?" Trainer Shion asks.

"Personal reasons. Nothing illegal or harmful." That's an excuse that unsticks most social jams, assuming you have built up enough social leverage. Which you have, since Trainer Shion sought to scout you and you took to her introductory lessons well enough.

"Alright. Might change the latter if her best pal's involved, but whatever. Cafe's not the recluse she used to be. She can hold down a conversation." Trainer Shion reaches into a box and pops another jellybean. "So, spill it. The reason you're here and not with her."

There's an edge to her tone now. Defensiveness. No Trainer, the good ones at least, will ever shy away from a threat to their trainee. Still, it's not as awkward as your second meeting with her, where the aforementioned request to scrim with Rice Shower happened. You were somewhat afraid that Trainer Shion got pissed with you for turning her down in favor of Kaori. She acted normally back then, which you deduced she accepted your denial as a fact of the industry and moved on with her life. You force yourself not to gulp and explain the chase for Manhattan Cafe, reducing your chasing as mere wandering and refraining from talking about souls and the Nightmare.

Trainer Shion absorbs the story. She clicks her tongue. She dumps half a dozen jellybeans on your open palms and watches you eat one before speaking. "Ruby, I hate to be the bearer of bad news, and no offence either, since you're a lovely girl and so are mine and Hiromi's, but if Cafe's been constantly avoiding you, doesn't that means she doesn't want to meet you?"

You lift a finger. "That has popped into my mind."

"You said you traversed a bunch of rooms. And none of the other girls there said Cafe was recently there, like a minute ago?"

"It was half-half, I think."

"Maybe it's time to give up the ghost. Find another girl to hang out with. Tracen's wide as the ocean; hell, I could introduce you to one of Rice's new friends."

[Persuasion check: 114/55 -> Success! Trivia: +0 EXP.]

"But it makes no sense!" You protest.

"Why?" Trainer Shion says.

"Because I've never met Manhattan Cafe before. And I'm dead sure she doesn't hate me back, otherwise you wouldn't have scouted me in the first place."

Trainer Shion pauses. She glances to the side. "Fair point."

You clasp your hands. "Please, Trainer Shion! I need to meet Cafe for…"

Hold on. What is your excuse here? You better answer fast, or else Trainer Shion will think something is wrong…

(What's your excuse? Choose only one.)

[] [DailyLife4] I, too, am a connoisseur of coffee.

[] [DailyLife4] I really admire her running. Her Kikuka Sho brought tears to my eyes and it's all cool and sad and please just let me see her.

[] [DailyLife4] She's my long-lost childhood friend.

[] [DailyLife4] She's magical and I'm interested in that,

[] [DailyLife4] I must prove my annoying Senpai wrong.

[] [DailyLife4] I have a letter that must be delivered in person.

[] [DailyLife4] I have a crush on her.

[] Write-in.

Noon, July 5th, 20XX

Your prize is an omamori. It's a specific breed of good-luck charm often sold at shrines. Wrapped in a pine-green cloth and embroidered with gold stalks and leaves down the side, the inscription reads out a mantra of good fortune and health.

How appropriate. Right in time for your debut.

You turn the item over in your palm, then clench it, closing your eyes. Plain Jane mentioned all objects possess souls, from the tiniest blade of grass to the most glorious conqueror of empires. The more individualized, the stronger the soul is. The omamori is likely mass-produced, woven and built together in a factory instead of the lineup you produced by hand back in the countryside.

It is due to this that you cannot detect the tiny smidgen of its soul. That could change in the future, assuming you lavish the same amount of care and attention as you gave your trusty silver bullet. That thing used to be nothing more than a hunk of mysterious metal. The silver bullet and the minty green omamori can be charm buddies. Or charm marriage partners? You'll have to revisit your closet and select a few other mini-ornaments in your wardrobe.

For now, you'll hang it from your bag's zipper, where it'll look cute.

[All Magical Disciplines have increased by 5!]

[EXP Gained: 35.]

Total EXP: 215/220

5.3: Daily Life VIII

>>[DailyLife1] Interrupt and ease Tabaru into facing her fears.

>>[DailyLife2] Attempt to calm Oguri down.

>>[DailyLife3Part1] Yes, No, Maybe? It shouldn't have gotten that bad and I'm glad to help, but it needs a more permanent solution

>>[DailyLife3Part2] Apologise for swearing.

>>[DailyLife4] She's magical and I'm interested in that,

EXP: 215/220

Mood: Good

Afternoon, June 27th, 20XX

The situation in the parlor unfolds, less like a delicate flower opening its buds and more akin to a grenade exploding slow-mo inside some run-down public cinema screen. Gold Ship is the centerpiece. The key culprit. Because of course she is. If it's not the mystifying glow radiating out of her soul's core, it's her posture. Look at her. Hands tucked behind her head, back leaning relaxed against the seat. Glibness in every square centimeter of fibre. That sturdy square jaw swings on its hinges of bone and sinew as she rambles on and on about her grand plans for Tabaru's debut.

"Ooh! Let's do an ochazuke roulette, too! We haven't had one of those in ages, right, Tabaru?"

You attempt to summon courage in your throat. To ask what the crud green tea on rice has to do with this, and can we please all calm our cleats and get back on track? Futile. It's futile. Vividness waterfalls straight from Gold Ship's gums; it slices through the white noise whine through your head and beams images in a finished manga manuscript format. A balloon float. A buffet of carrots and gravy, Trainer Nase received the sack, thirty purple tentacles that smell of grape jelly, a burger so tall it reaches the top of the academy flagpole. These are the celebrations, and then there's the immediate aftermath of the race. On the turf, shadowed by raining confetti, a dozen sisters and cousins gather around Tabaru and clap their hands. That 'Lila' and 'Marche' are there—dusky-rose with a white dot and polite applause for the former, a pinkish-red hand puppet that's cheering wildly for the latter. This is exactly what they look like. You've never set a single foot in Gold Clan territory before, yet you know this to be true.

Instead of being horrified at these illusions, or at the very least frightened at the sheer amount of waste of money…

[World Resonance check: 108/200 -> Failure.]

You find yourself entranced, as if you're huddled in the pit, watching the latest underground show for free (being an umadol has its perks).

The illusion fragments when Gold Ship mentions hiring a singer from UKB48. The gag reflex activates. Please. The latest generation is so not the 19XX crop, no matter how hard they try to pretend to be. You've heard bargain bin vinyls in second-hand Akihabara radio stores with more soul than the 20XX trash. That flex of disgust is the backhand that snaps you awake. You tremble in your seat, flushed with embarrassment and shame that you let yourself get caught wasting so much time.

"They're gonna be there. They're gonna see me…"

Next to you, frantic mumbles pour out of a shivering Tabaru. A closer glance at her, and the alarm bells shatter their glass cages. Her upper incisors press down on her lip. The indent is wide enough that you can smell the blood bleeding iron from the future wound.

"If I don't win by at least two—no, three lengths. Gotta get an early gate start too. Then, I…I…"

"Long story short, we've got money to splurge, and my Trainer to beg if we need more snacks and park tickets. He might look scary, but don'tcha worry. He's a total pushover. We just gotta say it's for joint training, and if that doesn't work, we can threaten to star him in a viral vid idea! Numbers 2 and 3 should work."

A pure wave of dread for the sake of Trainer Okino surges through you.

"Boo-yah! This is going to be great!" Gold Ship slams her arms wide. "You've got this, Tabaru!"

Tabaru curls in her seat and gazes wistfully into her melting ice-cream cup.

"Right, Tabaru?"

"I…I…"

"Is that a yes? Going once, going twice…"

Code red. Red of the crimson of spilled blood. Captain, captain, you think with the distant hum of a rumbling stick of dynamite, we are imminent for a crash-landing into a crater labelled total and utter annihilation.

Does Gold Ship not understand what she's doing here? Is Gold Ship that oblivious to her little cousin undergoing a mental breakdown over here? Or is this some deliberate Gold Clan ploy? It's enough to make a good uma howl. You are suddenly struck with a thought. Goodness, is this what Mejiro McQueen deals with every day? Setting aside her relationship with your estranged sisters and her inability to perceive the magical side of reality, you've always shared the private opinion that McQueen was too pompous and shackled to the Mejiro duty for her own good. Right now, you're starting to view her as a saintess in hiding. Tosen Jordan can at least book it out of the room whenever Gold Ship shows up. McQueen is bound to Gold Ship on account of them existing on the same team. McQueen's patience must be enormous nowadays, or she's learned how to cock an ear without switching her brain on to actually listen.

Anyway, for the sake of your roommate's sanity, you have to interfere. Now!

"Hold on a damn second!"

Your voice explodes, louder than you intended. Several other parlor-goers swivel their heads to stare. You shoot them with a mildly offended look, and they return to minding their own business without issue.

"What's cooking, babycakes?" Gold Ship asks.

You clear your throat. "Sorry. That was a…" You twist your mouth as you think for a suitable adverb. "Lovely speech you made, Gold Ship."

"Aw, you're sweet."

"Anyway, I just wanted to say…" You brace yourself for the second impact. A shiver down your spine. Your back muscles tense up. Here comes the intake of oxygen. "You're going way overboard!"

"Eh?" Gold Ship's eyes widen. She recoils, thrashing her body, "But I packed my life raft in my luggage last night! Is this a mutiny? We scuttling the ship, captain?"

Don't question that, you tell yourself. Don't even think about those metaphors. You continue pointing an accusing finger at Gold Ship. "A float parade? A whole buffet? Pissing off Trainer Nase, of all people? Are you trying to bring down the entire academy and the URA-centric press on Tabby's head? It's just a debut, for crying out loud."

Gold Ship rolls her eyes. "C'mon, we're obviously not gonna go ahead with every single one of those. I was throwing out ideas, that's all."

"Any one of them would be considered too much for a G1!" You say.

This causes Gold Ship to rest an elbow on her table. "Hey, hey, listen to yourself. Put respect on the name. Who's got multiple Takarazukas under her belt here?"

A score in her favor. Unfortunately for her, you possess the easiest counter in the world. 'At least I didn't throw away billions of yen by screwing around!' you can scream and strike at the heart of Gold Ship's ego, angering her beyond reproach and massacring any chance of negotiations to a bloody halt. So, not helpful in the slightest, aside from indicating how ticked off you are. Second plan, then.

You whip out your mobile phone and jab at the center of the screen. It flickers on, revealing a wallpaper of a band you liked two days ago, but now think is cringe. You quickly slam your thumb on the power button and put it back into rest mode. "I have a friend called Umagle. She fetches me articles straight from the Web, informing me how most teams celebrate G1s. Most of the time, it's more basic than the public imagines. For example, Kaori took Jordan to a big restaurant with her friends and a couple of important sponsorships. They chatted a bunch, gorged themselves silly, and at the end Jordan received a bunch of expensive gifts. That was it."

"That's Jordan though…" Gold Ship muses. "Her Trainer's got her on a tight leash."

"Point stands. You splurge too hard and it'll overwhelm poor Tabaru. Especially after she's run two thousand meters in front of a national-level crowd."

You pat Tabaru on the shoulder. A vibration runs up your fingers, which is a sign she's listening, you hope.

Gold Ship shrugs. "Got half a dozen of us and more. Each one of us has their own tastes and ways to party. They're finicky about their preferences."

Or is that her preferences she's talking about?

"Seriously, you try telling Journey she's not allowed to hold her tea ceremonies. I'll be waking up in the middle of an Ikebukuro alleyway with my kidneys stolen," Gold Ship lifts a hand, stretching the five fingers straight. "Tell ya what, sweet-cheeks. Down to fifty percent. Final deal."

"That's still a lot. You can organize it within the span of a week?"

Gold Ship retracts her hand. She pushes her fist into palm, cracks her knuckles and smirks. "It's simply how the town swings, baby, and I'm an uma of my word. Ring-a-ding-ding!"

She then blasts you with the finger-guns. The core of the soul's radiance melts into the smoky orange of loose shredded peels and the portrait of a solar flare. The acrid gunpowder blows through the air, stinging your nostrils. The twitch in your right shoulder is Tabaru shooting you a sympathetic glance, probably. You find yourself with the energy to the chest, stiff in your chair, blank-faced outside, quaking inside as if Gold Ship pulled out a Glock or whatever guns they use in the JSDF and blasted you in the chest. Had she been a real Horror from the Nightmare, there's no way you would've survived that horrendous shadow race.

This line of argument is a wash. Gold Ship will not budge. She believes within the bedrock of her heart that Tabaru will win, therefore the celebrations are on. It'd be heartwarming if you weren't attempting to out-debate her.

Wait.

[Logic check: 93/50 -> Success! +5 EXP.]

Gold Ship thinks Tabaru will win? When was that ever established?

From the beginning, your mind answers. It's the crux of the argument. Moron. The more you repeat it, the more off it feels. You keep thinking about it as you shove half-melted ice-cream down your gullet for the sugar replenishment, and out of nowhere, a lightbulb flashes on inside your head.

The idea you've come up with is risky. It is volatile. And it's not based on known reality, which is the actual most dangerous aspect. Play this wrong, and you'll make an absolute fool of yourself.

"Ruby…" Tabaru speaks up. She grabs your arm. "It's okay. You don't have to…"

"I've got this, Tabby," you reply.

Gold Ship stands up. She pushes her chair in. She circles around the table and presses Tabaru close to her. Tabaru's face goes into her chest, softly this time, and no struggle is present. A vein pulses in your forehead. This is stuff you already understand, as a former umadol. It's apparent to anyone in Tracen with half a brain. You hold your tongue, because Tabaru is listening, enraptured.

Obscene slurps sound. A few trickles of vanilla and chocolate dribble down the side of Tabaru's mouth and chin. She holds the cup for a few seconds, her eyes obscured by her falling twintails and the girth of the cup's glass. Calories. More unwanted calories. Kaori can sniff out traces of sugar and frosting from a kilometer away—they don't call her Tracen's Pastry Queen around the staff lounge for nothing. You're bargaining with Gold Ship, pulling up the menu, gesturing at the kilojoule ratings as Gold Ship leans back and recites a tale about Mejiro McQueen in the old grandmotherly voice, and you slam the menu down and suddenly realise with a jolt the whole ordeal with Tabaru was wiped from your mind briefly in favor of arguing with Gold Ship, wiping away the stress you yourself felt, and now she and Tabaru are giggling and laughing together like a pair of matching bells.

Gold Ship winks at you. Another vein throbs. Then, Tabaru catches your eye. She mouths two single words.

Thanks, Ruby.

You gingerly raise your hand for a thumbs-up. No worries, Tabby. I've got your back.

Machan shrugs. It's a rhetorical question you're asking, the motion says. You raise a finger, then drop it. Then, you slouch back in your seat with a growl and a pout. Manager Suzuki waited for your ire to fade, then told you he was informing you of this to be more considerate of older fans and clients. That was it, so stop jumping up, thank you very much.

The conversation lulls. You slouch in your seat, a muted, half-asleep position. The faded patterns on the wallpaper ahead splatter like ink blots. Blood patterns under a microscope. One finger digs into a hole in the seat's fabric and rolls around the tufts of cloth there. Sandpaper on your rough fingers. Slowly, gradually, a chill creeps up to fill the vacuum left behind the vacant hype. Goosebumps erupt on your bare skin.

Machan crawls over. She examines you without touching, like the apprentice nurse you imagine her to be. She grabs your coat out of your bag and drapes it over you, then presses the plush doll of herself into your arms. This must be harrowing for her, you muse inside your head, for her to let go of that precious toy. Not a single stitch is out of place. Most of the time, she's flagging the doll to any camera that catches her attention in an effort to ensure she's remembered for eternity.

It's a curious dream of hers. You've tasted a bit of it, as an umadol, though to a far greater extent on the more infamous end as Satono Opal's lone daughter. Machan drags you over to a vending machine and purchases hot chocolates for the two of you. Skim milk. No real sugar. You sip yours with Machan's personal doll still tucked under one elbow. Assuming that's still on the menu.

Not that it's a hard problem. You've already established that few girls in Tracen have the capability to pinpoint that many pain points in a shrine's upkeep.

So, you spill. You tell her that you were a former miko. That your expertise in cleaning the shrine originated from the many years you spent sweeping, cleaning, and refurbishing a lonely little shrine deep in the Japanese countryside. It's impossible to spend that much time without feeling the aftereffects. The modern city sank its hooks into you, yet the muscle memory lingers. You have enough expertise that you could pass the Association of Shinto Shrines' qualification exam on your first go.

This makes Machan the second uma in Tracen you've told this to. She doesn't look very surprised.

"So that old groundskeeper reminded you of the head priest?" Machan asks.

"Your surrogate?" Realisation flashes in Machan's round eyes. "Oh, Ruby, I'm so sorry. I take it she wasn't so kind to you?"

An understatement, you snicker. The woman had it out for you the moment you stepped onto the front porch. Told you to throw away the fancy dress your mother had damn-near vandalized a children's clothing store for the red-white miko uniform. Told you the next day to pick up the broom and start sweeping. Two hands and two legs—there was no excuse. Reprimands for practically everything; the best you got in the matter of praise were curt nods. It wasn't a case of her being strict, like a drill sergeant, or a stone-faced teacher, because there were times, multiple times, when you followed her instructions to the letter, only for her to spring out some unexpected or completely new fault upon you, before ordering you to fix it on the spot.

Then, there was kegare. Machan doesn't get it, so you explain. Uncleanliness made manifest, normally reserved for spiritual uncleanliness and pollution, like puddles after a storm. Except they reserved it for a small child. "At least it wasn't the type where I had to pretend she and I were related by blood."

Morning, July 4th, 20XX

"Because Cafe is magical!" you cry out.

Trainer Shion wrinkles her nose. She folds her arms and gives you a good, long stare. It's the type that pins your words back onto yourself, settles them, and gradually causes a sinking feeling to settle in your abdomen.

"You wanna back that up, Ruby?"

"No, I'm serious," you say and fold your arms in response, "I'm totally, totally, serious!"

"How?"

"Um…"

The inky coffee-stained shadows follow in her wake—a happenstance you have not yet fully confirmed? Yeah, sure. Give more reasons for this already doubtful maid to doubt you more. Instead, you tell Trainer Shion a bunch of facts about her own Trainee. Manhattan Cafe is indeed magical, in the sense that her stamina and ability to run long-distance races are almost unmatched in Tracen. She's also a fantastic case of achieving success despite an ailing body. With the breadth of your studies and some PR speak thrown into the mix, it's easy to rattle off a short speech about how you were inspired by her patience and tenacity in the Arima Kinen and hope you can ask her for some advice on how to apply that to your own long-distance races.

"…Fine," Trainer Shion says.

"You serious?"

"Despite my hunch that your search for Cafe involves reasons beyond learning from her, I can't deny you put in a good pitch. You'll also track her down to her dorm room if I refuse to entertain you and then I'll have an even bigger headache to deal with."

"Hey!" you say, "I'm no stalker."

"Right, right, but I've also been a Tracen Trainer for years. Word around the lounge is that you can't verify squat without seeing it with your own two eyes. Second word is that hormones plus tight competition multiplied by teenage drama means war," Trainer Shion says. She scratches her cheek and yawns. "I'll attempt to set up a time and place. The keyword is attempt. It's up to Cafe to agree. If she doesn't, I'm gonna respect her volition and decline your request. Peace?"

"Thank you very much!" You bow your head, causing Trainer Shion to click her tongue and grumble about Cafe needing to leave her room more often.

So, you go back to your regular life, awaiting the message from Trainer Shion. It arrives swiftly, surprisingly enough. Four o'clock in the afternoon, in an empty classroom on the third floor of the building. A curious place for a meeting. You would've chosen the library or a bench under the shade, like the meeting you had with Agnes Digital, but beggars cannot be choosers. After clearing this meeting with Kaori, you head to the designated meeting place.

Manhattan Cafe is not here. Instead, the other Trainer of Team Eridanus is present: Maid Green—or to be more accurate: Trainer Hiromi—who picked up Pelte like it was nothing and then blitzed it to the infirmary weeks ago. You catch her fidgeting with her hands as you enter.

"H-hello!" She perks up as you enter. "Hi, Ruby!"

"Hi, Trainer Hiromi," you say. You look around. Empty desks, empty tables, closed windows. Zero sources of inky, coffee-stained shadows. "Is Cafe here?"

In response, Hiromi steps aside and gestures to the desk behind her. An object rests in the center. You stare at it. You behold it. The action is deliberate. This is due to the object being a metal box the size of a fruit package crate. Its heavy lid is bound shut by loops of chain and steel wire. Several locks, of the analog and digital variety, add another layer of security. You approach it, whereupon your nose twitches at the bitter scent of cold, industrial rust.

Pure confusion washes over you. The crate belongs more in the prop department of a movie set, instead of Tracen's furniture & equipment supply. It is also, importantly, not large enough to fit an uma the size of Manhattan Cafe.

"What is this?" You ask.

"Well, Shion passed on the message to Cafe that you wanted to see her." Trainer Hiromi says.

"And?"

Trainer Hiromi nods down to the box.

"She sent me this in response?"

Trainer Hiromi nods again. Her long matcha-latte-green twintails bounce like flapping wings.

"And she expects me to now… open this?"

A third nod.

You stare again. You ask Hiromi again. She nods, even yet again. And this is when you are gripped, seized like an iron maiden in motion, by the urge to yank Trainer Hiromi by the shoulders, drag her over to the stupid box and shake her up and down, asking if she is kidding herself, what does she even mean, this is not how Manhattan Cafe acts according to her socmed, and is there a hidden camera recording up in the ceiling tiles, ready to snap and sell pics of your open hanging, mouth? An uma assaulting a human is a fast ticket to ending up in front of a courtroom or, worse, expulsion from Tracen.

Besides, it's probably best not to offend the woman who could probably tear a stone pillar in half with her bare hands. You end up holding your head and wondering how hard Plain Jane is laughing in the Shadow Paddock.

"If it's any consolation…" Trainer Hiromi begins, and you immediately think her next words shall not be anything of the sort, "Cafe did promise a meeting would occur if you successfully opened the box."

"Did she?" You murmur.

"She rarely lies to Shion or me."

"That's…reassuring. I guess?"

"She also asked her friends to pitch in with the locks too! Look."

Trainer Hiromi pulls out a specific lock on the box. You squint at it. Instead of numbers, there are…

"Chemistry symbols?"

"That's from Miss Tachyon."

H, Li, Be—periodic symbols. The sight of them reminds you of the periodic table and your repeated efforts to memorize it in class, all of which have ended in repeated failure. The damage is immerse. Your mind staggers back and hides under its blankets for comfort.

"Why?" You mutter to yourself. "Is this something Manhattan Cafe does nowadays?"

"Sorry," Trainer Hiromi mumbles. "I should've asked Shion to meet you."

"No, no, that's fine…" you groan. Somehow, you suspect she had a role to play in springing this trap. In hindsight, she wasn't super enthused about the idea of you meeting Cafe. "Thanks for obliging me with this…"

The sad fact is that you can't muster up the energy to be spiteful.

Trainer Hiromi is compassionate enough to help you haul the box back to your dorm room. Once inside, you shove the box into the back of your closet, a good distance away from your hanging uniform sets. This stupid thing does not deserve to rest under the bed alongside your mother's shoes.

You slump face-down onto your bed.

This is the result of your hard work. This is how the great Manhattan Cafe behaves. Reclusive, suspicious, and now malicious enough to lead an innocent, young uma along, then slam the door on her face at the last second with a…an… escape room puzzle? A video game set piece? Whatever it is, its presence is an act of malice. It's a trick you'd expect from Plain Jane, because she's mysterious and super old and thus the type to push puzzles into young umas' faces for her twisted amusement. If not her, one of your senpais dripping with a monarch's arrogance, such as Orfevre or Gentildonna. Even then, those two would at least tell you to shove off to your face.

It doesn't fit. It feels out of character for Cafe. Did she even send this to you? Is Trainer Shion the real culprit here?

[Instinct check: 43/80 -> Failure.]

You don't know. The box gives off bad vibes, but that's due to it looking like a piece of gutter trash. It is also lacking the inky-black shadows you associated with Cafe, which could be due to any number of reasons.

Weary down to your bones, you roll onto your side. You grab Trainer Hiromi's paper and unfold it for a quick look. It contains hints. Five for the five locks present on the box, once again confirming that this is a game. You're tempted to scrunch up the paper and hurl it into your bin. Alas, the natural curiosity that kept you alive on the streets takes hold, and you read the rest of the paper.

The hints…

[Wits check: 10/9 -> Success! +10 EXP.]

…aren't too hard to parse. Unlocking the box might be possible if you settle down and give it a proper go…

Noon, July 7th, 20XX

"Oguri. Oguri!"

Oguri Cap is not at home. She is currently wearing the mask of a raging bull lacking its matador. Gnashed teeth, fuming nostrils, her feet slam into the grass as if it's the turf and she's performing one of her famous spurts. Please hold.

"Oguri!" You shout again. You grab her sleeve, tugging her towards you. Oguri doesn't budge, so you grit your teeth and try again. It's like trying to pull a boulder with a headphone cord. "It's fine. You hear me? It's fine. I'm fine!"

Oguri wrenches her neck to look aside at you. "They hurt you, Ruby!"

"They tried to hurt me. They failed," you correct her. "I'm unharmed."

"They had no care for what they were about to do. I saw them! They could've given you a concussion. Broken your hip. Your spine! They could have crippled you!" Oguri roars back.

You deliberately wince and incline your neck back so that Oguri knows how unnecessarily loud she's being. It works. Her features soften by a small amount. You take the opportunity to grab her by both shoulders and swing her around with all your might.

[Power check: 10/10 -> Success! +10 EXP.]

It's a success. Oguri stops facing the bullies. She's seeing the full picture—yourself. Hair sticking out at a few ends, and a smattering of grass strands and dirt spots on your uniform. Mere cosmetic damage. There's a complete lack of blood or bruising.

"See?"

Oguri steps forward. She examines you once, then twice, then thrice. She goes as far as to pull at your sleeves and collar to check your skin. The motions are rough and frantic. She stops after checking your abdomen—you rolled up your top for that one—whereupon she takes a shuddering breath. The rage roiling inside her quells.

You squirm with your own dawning relief. Oguri won't physically assault the trio of bullies now. A part of you knew she obviously wasn't about to do that, but another part recognised Oguri's rage as at the same level as yours, during that attempted theft of your mother's shoes by that drunk.

Just because physical punishment is off the table doesn't mean Oguri is in the mood for mercy. She rips her phone out of her pocket and punches in a number.

"Air Groove, it's me. A trio tried to severely harm Satono Ruby behind Academy Main Building C. Deal with them."

A squawk of annoyance bleats from the other line.

"I don't give a damn about your meeting. A student was almost crippled out of their career and no one knew about it. The patrols and the supervising teachers need a massive overhaul. Get over here! Now!"

Only the Grey Beast herself could order the Empress around and not be slammed into detention.

Oguri snaps her flip-phone shut. The fangirl, the lead bully who had organized this whole mess, finally breaks out of her trance. She collapses onto the grass. Head tipped back, nostrils leaking; a wave of fat, ugly tears roll down her cheeks. She clutches herself and sobs. Her friends glance at each other, hopeless.

And Oguri, the uma whom she joined Tracen for in the first place, shoots her a contemptous look reserved for roadkill vermin.

"Stay there," she orders.

They will. The fight has long since fled them.

You're not around to witness Air Groove's arrival. Oguri grabs you by the arm and drags you away. You are unable to protest.

Destination: Oguri Cap's Ritto dorm room. The dorm clerk is barely given a moment's notice before she storms through the lobby and up the steps, you trailing behind and shooting an apologetic glance behind. A punch of a PIN code, and you're in. The understanding that you have entered the Oguri Cap's private room hits you seconds after the door closes. Yet again, Satono Ruby has received a privilege thousands of URA fans would sell their left kidneys for. You should be intimidated, or at least awestruck enough to ask for a private photo. Not anxious. Not afraid that Oguri hasn't spoken a single word on the way here.

Bottle in your face. Carrot juice straight from Oguri Cap's miniature fridge. The sight of the cool liquid sends the insides of your mouth moaning with thirst. You accept the drink, crack it open, and take a swig of the juice. It's faintly sweet. It's heaven. One swig falls into another, then a full-on chug. Oguri does the same. Two umas sitting in a room that should be a dozen times more elaborate with decorations and luxuries than it is, drinking juice and avoiding breaching the heaviness that strains between them.

Oguri finishes first. She hurls her bottle into a bin. She gazes into the paper wrappings and plastic waste lying inside. A direction away from the photos on her shelf, of Trainer Kitahara, Belno Light, an old man that is surely Trainer Musaka, and Oguri's numerous friends and acquaintances.

"So, um…" You have never been less fearful of breaking silence.

"Ruby," Oguri says. Her tone is soft. Deathly serious.

"Yeah? What's up?"

"Are you okay?"

"Me? Am I okay? Yeah. Yeah, I'm okay. I'm not hurt. Sheesh, I should be asking you that. Are you okay?"

"How long has this been going on?"

"Pardon?"

Oguri closes the distance. Her brow is creased with worry. "How long have you been bullied like that?"

You glance aside.

"Please. Tell me the truth."

"It's a long story. But, basically, ever since I entered Tracen?"

Oguri flinches, her teeth clenching. You hurry along before she breaks a molar.

"But it's eased quite a bit after the tryouts. Since I almost beat Kitasan, it's proven my skills are the real deal. It's told the hecklers that I'm here to stay in an official capacity. It's honestly not been so bad! I'm making progress." You lift a finger, putting on a grin. "Though, I guess there's always a bunch of sore losers amongst the crowd."

The awkward silence returns. You tap your foot, fidgeting.

"I've gotten used to it," you add. "This is nothing new."

"They could have crippled you," Oguri says, her voice hoarse. She slams her fist into the nearby closet, causing you to jump. "God. I can't believe it. I can't believe myself. That's coming out of your mouth without any hint of irony. That's your normal, Ruby, and it's my fault!"

"What?" You exclaim, raising your hands. "Oguri! What are you saying? No, how could that be possible? You've helped me. That tour you did, going around to show me off to your friends—it got the bullies off my back. They couldn't do squat when you were around. You were sorta acting like my bodyguard."

She snorts. "For all the good that did."

"And then there was that weekend disaster? Remember that? If you hadn't been there to comfort me, I might've dropped out of Tracen by now! Okay, so you're not my bodyguard. You can be my savior. That's cool, too."

Oguri brushes past you. She heads over to her closet. She flings the doors open. She crouches down and digs beneath the wall of uniforms on the coat hangers.

She returns, bearing a gift-wrapped box with a red ribbon tied in a neat bow up top.

"Thanks?" You ask.

Oguri doesn't hand it over. She stares at the box, her eyes shadowed. "Ruby. Do you remember the first day we met?"

You blink, tilting your head. "Of course I do. It was the best first real race I could've asked for."

"You ever wondered why I was there?"

"What do you mean?"

"You and I had never met at that point, yet I knew exactly where you were. Did you even wonder how I knew?

You pause. "Because Rudolf told you?"

Oguri shakes her head. "She didn't. She told only Grass."

You hum as you dig through your memories. "Didn't you say you asked the Vice-Prez?"

"And why was I asking her and able to arrive where you were on the dot?"

"Because you've so attentive?"

Oguri gives a bitter half-smirk. "You could say that."

You pout. "The heck do you want me to say? It's not like there was a conspiracy against me to, what, add another runner to my first race. Not from you, of all umas."

Seriously, can this legend stop putting herself down for five seconds? It's becoming tiresome, especially when she's done the opposite of deserving such self-deprecation. Ugh, should you call Digital now? She'd leap out of class to clear Oguri up in a jiffy. You're not qualified to handle this moody Oguri Cap.

You examine the gift box. On the surface, it's ordinary. Cute, even, with the wrapping paper styled in little polka dots, and the ribbon seal up top adorned with a cloth flower. It's exactly the gift you wished you could've received on Christmas Day, as you held up signs and watched couples hold hands beneath twinkling lights and walk down the lanes holding hands. Americans have it so good with their public holidays.

"Bit too early, isn't it?" You comment.

Oguri disagrees. She hands the box over to you.

The moment touches your hands, your chest aches. A small flutter, the act of the heart skipping a beat, so rapid it catches you off guard and causes you to splutter. A tightness constricts your abdomen; you almost drop the gift in surprise.

No. You can't. You can't do that. The wrapping paper isn't slippery, for one. What are you doing—

The gift vibrates. Vibrates through you. Silver trails and sparkles pop in and out of your vision. Your mind swims, churns, whirlpools. Stop it, your heart sings again. This is impolite. This is foolish of you. It could contain a trap. A bomb, a knife, a jester's box. Haven't you seen what happens when a soldier steps on a landmine and has to figure out how to escape in the movies? Hold the box down. Hold it until you can figure it out. The landmine was a metaphor. What's inside is much worse, much greater, much more precious than anything as meager as a weapon to harm you.

[World Resonance check: 108/50 -> Success! Trivial: +0 EXP.]

Eh?

Precious? Where did that word come from?

And when did your free hand clutch around your lucky trinket, as it thrums with the same thrill you feel at the beginning of a race?

"Hey, Oguri." Your head swims with clouds. You step closer to her. "What's inside this?"

Oguri takes a deep breath and tells you.

>>OGURI CAP'S SPECIAL: BEGIN.

5.4: That Leap (Bonus)

Total words: 18000+

Takes place from before the quest's beginning up until 2.6.

PART 1

After the Winning Live, it's the usual song and dance. Oguri walks up the steps onto the stage platform. She plonks herself down on a plastic chair, inspecting the press table laid out before her. It's the familiar setup: microphone in front, bottles of water to her left, a crowd of eager journalists in their jackets and slacks up front. Dozens of cameras click, their silvery flashes bouncing off the checkerboard green-and-white wall and causing her to squint mildly, as always.

She'd ask them to cut it out if she wasn't flush with victory. Sitting beneath the spotlight, tasting the intertwined scents of high-quality air freshener and her own hearty sweat, as thousands upon thousands beam at her through the bulky cameras—she's never been a fame chaser, nor a money-hungry hound, but she can recognize that this is the winner's privilege, the one out of the thirteen, and it's all hers.

It's energizing. It replaces the exhaustion from her prior race's now cooled-off high. She faces the crowd with a steady, but not too deep, breath and puts on her best friendly smile.

She doesn't know there's a man in the crowd, wrapping his sweaty fingers around a deadly grenade.

"Oguri Cap! Oguri Cap!" A journalist—a woman in a brown flat cap—raises her hand. "Congrats on your victory. We were all awestruck by your performance from start to finish. Call you tell us: has it sunk in yet for you?"

Oguri leans forward to grab the microphone. The crowd of journalists incline in turn.

"If the win hasn't hit me yet, then it hasn't happened, which means this is all a dream!" Oguri says and smiles, prompting a round of chuckles. "But, yeah, for real—it has. I'm incredibly satisfied with my victory, and it couldn't have happened under better conditions or with a better lineup of rivals. They gave it their absolute best. So did I. Now, I won't speak for them, since they're perfectly capable of that themselves, but at the very least, I have no regrets."

She lets familiar faces flash through her mind. "Needless to say, they'll be raring to go the next time we clash on the turf. So I won't be slacking off. I'll apply what I learned today to my next race."

Pleased murmurs circulate around the crowd. The lady journalist nods and writes something down on her notepad. On the side, one Belno Light gives a thumbs-up from the shadows of the right wing, while Trainer Ginjirou Musaka nods approvingly, trying not to look too pleased.

Another journalist takes the stand. "Talk us through that final stretch. What did you see in that final section of the homestretch?"

"Nothing short of pure brilliance," Oguri responds. "It was as if Tamamo's mind and mine were electrifying each other, yet resonating as one."

"Did any of your opponents' tactics catch you off guard?" a third asks.

"Well…I was a bit surprised when Creek came charging in. Sorry, that's bad manners of me. I shouldn't have mentioned that," Oguri coughs into her hand. "Apologies. It was a good move, though. Creek is an amazing stayer. No disrespect to her."

"You're looking especially fresh today, Oguri Cap. What's the secret to your composure? On or off the track, please. The world's salivating to know!" calls the fourth.

"C'mon, I'm not that great," Oguri says.

"Nah, you're spectacular!" Someone else calls from the back of the audience. Another round of laughs. All in good fun, of course. Oguri shrugs and provides some general pointers from her own experience: a few books her Trainer and Belno directed her to in the past, the general headspace she tries to slide herself into before a match, and the concept of always believing yourself deserving of victory while not underestimating your opponent, and so on and so forth. It was a good question. Patience is the underappreciated tool attached to the star athlete's belt. If her question can get the competition to not bolt the moment she pushes on the pedal and grant her a better playing field to fight in, all the better.

The rest of the press release flows. Oguri smiles and waves at the crowd. She takes sips of water from the bottles, because that's what they are for. People want the expected and the unexpected; the balance is to reveal information they should and could know, had they possessed infinite time to think over the question themselves. Always, always respect your opponents, even if you wanted to stop time and break their nose while you were on the turf. The journalists scribble down their notes and beg for more.

Things are going well. They're going great. Oguri's on fire with these words, a linguistic inferno as if her racing skills were transplanted elsewhere. Behind her waving hands, she gets on her knees and thanks the Tracen faculty for seeing she once had as much charisma as a stinking fish and hiring Gold City to fix her attitude. Someone's getting a gift basket upon return.

Nothing could go wrong.

Nothing should do wrong.

Until the last five minutes, that's the status quo.

The press release is reaching the end. Oguri has chugged through three bottles of water. The back of her neck is sweating from the bright lights; the rest of the crowd isn't looking too solid, either. She's ready to board the train back to Fuchu, maybe sneak a tub or two of the new KFC buffet for a late afternoon snack. The thought causes her to almost drool, saved in time by an imaginary Gold City's smack.

This is when the man appears.

Oguri does not recognize him. Her keen senses do not detect as a threat, nor an abnormality. The truth is, the man isn't much. In a dark grey suit, his hair frayed at the edges yet resembling the primness of a salaryman's short cut, he stumbles through the crowd, elbowing and getting elbowed back in turn, his steps bearing the feeble gait of a rookie in over his head. Oguri could pluck a handful of salarymen off Scramble Crossing and end up with six of these jokers.

She faces him with grace, regardless.

"Excuse me, Miss Oguri Cap…" the man begins.

"Yes?"

The man, the rookie, stammers for a second. Oguri decides she'll be more patient with this one. If she stretches it out enough, this could be the last question of the day.

"This is in regard to your friend and rival, Super Creek."

"Yeah, it's really tragic what happened to her. It wasn't really her fault; sometimes we get too overeager and rush to put our practice into motion. Happens to everybody. I don't begrudge her. Neither, I hope, will the rest of us."

"Exactly! You took the words out of my mouth! Thank you for that." The man exclaims. Color seeps into his pale pallor. He swallows a lump in his throat, smiling awkwardly. Oguri smiles back, raising her eyebrows slightly in anticipation.

The rookie lifts his head and pulls the pin on his grenade.

"Due to the nature of the disqualification, that being obstruction, we've been hearing rumors circulating amongst the fandom that she might be…um… similar in execution, or spirit, or nature to Satono Opal. What are your thoughts on this?"

Oguri blinks. She has no clue who this Satono Opal uma is.

The rest of the crowd begs to differ.

At first, the rookie is oblivious. His shoulders slump, an action of pure release and relief at finally saying what was brewing in his head. Then, he raises his head, looks around, and the fact that he just said what was brewing in his head smacks him over the head. Over a hundred pairs of eyes are now staring. The ones in his near vicinity: they stare harder. They glare. He tries to back away, only to slam into a wall of advancing bodies, atop which the faces contort into ghastly theatre masks of vengeance and rage.

"Um…" Oguri says.

She's the firing pistol. Hell breaks loose.

"What the hell did he say—"

"Kid, are you for real right now? Comparing Super Creek to her of all umas?"

"You thought it was sharp to bring this up after the Arima-fucking-Kinen?"

"Did your mom drop you on your head? Did your ancestors side with the Yanks? Do you have no shame?"

That last shout originates from one bearded older journalist in a top hat. Spittle flies, lands, and causes that patch of the crowd to go more incensed. The rookie cowers in his position, almost in the prone position. Froth trickles out of his mouth.

"Wait," Oguri cries. A high-pitched screech cuts through the air mid-sentence, causing her to wince. "Don't mob him. Please stop doing that—"

"You've got her worked up, you bastard!" a journalist roars at the poor man.

A wad of paper sails through the air and plonks the rookie on the head. It hits his head with a noticeable clunk. Security finally snaps out of their stupor and shoves the mob's edges to wade in. They're not fast enough—not that the rookie is beaten to unconsciousness, but that because another figure squirms through the mess and cuts the clamor short.

"Excuse me, excuse me!" The offending rookie lights up at hearing the voice, expecting rescue. His hair is seized by like a tuft of fabric, and the rest of his head is painfully forced down by the firm hand of one Fuiji Sensuke.

"Oguri, I am so, so sorry about this," Fuiji says towards the front stage. He shakes his head and bows his head, joining his young colleague. "This idiot—I don't know where or when he picked up that question—but he shouldn't have asked you that. Not in a million years!"

"Sensuke!" Musaka stomps forth. He slams his cane on the ground like a judge's hammer. His gravelly voice roars across the din. "What sort of manners are you teaching the brats down at your office?"

Fuiji faces Musaka.

This is a man who has never once backed down from a scoop, who is described by his colleagues as muckraking mercenary with a pallor as yellow as a moldy carpet, who broke off his own damn date to interview Oguri. He has blown off Musaka's wishes to eject himself into the nothingness every time he's swung by Tracen for an interview. Instead of a repeat at that, Fuiji tucks his chest in and bows low and deep towards Musaka.

"He's a rookie. He doesn't know a single difference between right and wrong. Bringing him here today was a mistake. I'll discipline him back to his senses when we return, I promise. Oguri Cap, Trainer Musaka, and the rest of the esteemed ladies and gentlemen here, please accept our and Umasporo Magazine's humblest apologies!"

He smacks the offending rookie when the latter stutters instead of apologizing with him.

198X, post Arima Kinen I. Post the day she defeated Tamamo Cross and cemented herself amongst the URA's best. Oguri Cap learns about Satono Opal for the first time in her life.

As she leaves the venue, the press release having been called off due to the mood being killed deader than an actual homicide victim, she spots a couple of compatriots amongst the crowd. Trainer Nase glares at Sensuke with the hurt she reserves for her estranged father. Maruzensky shakes her head wordlessly. Symboli Rudolf stares forward, her mouth pressed in a tight, contemplative line.

————

"Who's Satono Opal?" Oguri asks through a fresh bite of a KFC wing. Through the nearby window, the surrounding countryside zips by, a blur at the standard bullet train speed.

Musaka answers, "An uma who cheated in the Autumn Tenno Sho by covertly dismantling two runners' shoes and cleats in the changing rooms. One fell and broke her leg; the other injured her hips. They caught her after reviewing the footage in the hallways surrounding and inside the changing room."

Oguri's eyes widen. "That's terrible! No way Creek's as bad as someone like that!"

"I heard her scandal cut Tracen's attendance by half the following year," Belno chimes in, "The URA was seriously concerned about the future of the sport, too."

The fluorescent train lights reflect off Musaka's sunglasses, covering the thick darkness in a razor-sharp sheen. "She's ancient history, both of you. Nothing either of you should worry about. Forget about her and focus on yourself."

The severity in his tone shoves the question down Oguri's gullet, along with the mouthful of chicken and fried chicken skin. The silence lasts for the entire train ride back to Fuchu. Oguri has never heard Musaka speak in that tone, not even to his own nephew. What memory caused that? What uma could end up so nefarious, so dangerous, as to flip the switches of an entire room of normal people. Well, calling journalists normal is a stretch. It's not as if Satono Opal murdered anyone, did she?

Rudolf didn't look this troubled back when Oguri barged into her office to persuade her to let Oguri into the classics.

It might've been possible for Oguri to forget about this mysterious Satono Opal. Oguri is an obedient uma who listens to her Trainer. She is also a teenager who cannot help but dwell on a forbidden fruit. The more she tries to ignore it, the more it eats her mind from the inside. It shows via winces midway through running laps in training, costing her fractions of precious seconds.

Belno watches from afar. She notices Oguri's disrupted concentration. After some internal debate, she makes an executive decision.

Don't tell Musaka, the message attached to the Umatube video on LANE says. It's a link Oguri accepts gratefully.

That night, huddled up in her cozy blanket alone in her room, Oguri watches the video on a tiny phone screen. The documentary opens with a warning for graphic violence and unsettling content. It's a story of the URA—

A tale of Satono Opal—

A tale of highborn origins—

A trademark, irrefutable, madness-infused smugness amidst countless setbacks and iron-grit struggle—

—that concludes in the Tenno Sho, her greatest triumph—

—her and the URA's greatest disaster.

The cut to the victims flashbangs her in the face. Semi Sonic, sprawled on the turf behind a dozen other racers, clutches her shattered leg and howls for her mother. Nearby, Cotton Sphere tries to support herself on the railing, then falls.

Nausea rises up in Oguri's throat. The camera keeps rolling.

She sees Satono Opal, waving to the crowd, her ecstatic smile wrong at the edges. Satono Opal, escorted into her mansion by men in black suits amidst a furious press.
