"Yeah?" Oguri stammers. "What's the topic?"

"Satono Ruby," Tamamo says.

"Why are we talking about her?"

"I dunno. You seem close to her."

Oguri pales. She hopes the pile of food in front of her conceals her cheeks. "I'm not."

"You sure? Word on the street is that you're hanging around her these days," Tamamo says, "You wouldn't look bad next to her."

————

"What? Oguri, are—are you pulling my leg? I never told you to behave like a paparazzi! I just told you to be careful. You were meant to ease up once a week or two went by with nothing happening!" Folkqueen lets out a loud groan and slaps her face. Oguri winces at the audible noise. Behind Folkqueen lies the green room of some fashion show, with bright mirrors and bottles of expensive perfume. Muffled music plays in the background.

"Ugh, you're such a blockhead!" Folkqueen cries.

"I think…"

"No, you didn't. You didn't think. That's your whole problem in the first place!"

"I was trying to see if she was acting like Opal," Oguri mumbles.

"And why's that your responsibility? Even if she were, that's what the teachers are for!" Folkqueen shakes her head. "You better buy this Ruby chick an extra birthday cake because she has every right to slap you with a fan and call you a big, fat moron!"

————

Very few are privy to the information that Trainer Kitahara Jo tested the physical portion of Ruby's entrance exam.

"But are you sure she acted normal?"

"Yep. She was more nervous than anything. Almost believed like she'd fail, but she gathered up with her courage and pulled it off."

"And?"

"And what?"

"Anything else happened?"

"Why are you asking, Oguri?"

Oguri averts her gaze.

"Just curious. It's nothing."

"You and I both know that's not true," Kitahara pats a firm hand on Oguri's shoulder. "Come on. Tell me. I won't bite. I've always got time for you."

The grooves and vein lines on the back of Kitahara's hands grow more defined with each passing year. Oguri can't bear to meet her old Trainer's gaze.

————

Oguri ends up running to Rudolf. She opens her mouth and confesses what she's done. Shamefully, at first she tries to paint herself as a reasonable uma with rational goals that involve following a single uma and recording notes. She runs out of gusto halfway through and ends up pouring into a confession, her entire frame laden with a sinking feeling she has only ever felt in front of her mother or Trainer.

Rudolf doesn't scold her or write her up. She stands up from her desk and gestures Oguri to sit down on the comfortable pair of sofas in the middle of the room. Two glasses of cool tea are poured.

"What kind of person do you think Opal was?" Rudolf asks.

"A bad one," Oguri replies, listlessly. The tea is tasteless on her tongue.

"And if I suggested she should be rightfully punished by being sent to prison?"

"Depends on the criminal code for sabotage causing injury."

"And if the reason I ran at all was due to her?"

Oguri barely restrains herself from choking on her tea.

Rudolf smiles. "Just kidding. She didn't hold that much sway over my life."

Oguri doesn't laugh. She's not in the mood for humor today.

"I was acquainted with her at an early age, along with my childhood friends Sirius and Ramonu. By my estimate, she was almost in middle school when the three of us had just begun primary school level."

That tracks. The Symbolis, the Satonos, the Mejiros—these big, fancy conglomerates jostling for power and wealth. Their prospective heiresses were no doubt expected to mingle with each other as part of future social connections. It's one of those things Oguri has heard on the news, yet never once experienced.

Rudolf relaxes against the sofa's backrest. "The funny thing is, we never met Opal at some charity gathering."

Oguri nods. It's not often that Rudolf tells stories about her past. This one is about Opal, too. Despite the circumstances, Oguri finds herself interested.

"At least, not officially. Ramonu spotted this mysterious figure skulking around the premises, grumbling to herself, and pestered us to investigate. It turned out to be Opal in her dress, torn up at the edges, her shoes dented from sprinting, if I recall correctly, and she was holding a half-eaten burger in her hands."

Oguri raises her eyebrows. Rudolf chuckles to herself.

"That was the day I learned fast food existed, by the way."

"I believe you," Oguri says. It sounds like Opal, she almost says. The traitorous, wretched uma is portrayed so domestically Oguri can't help but squirm inside.

Rudolf continues speaking.

"Opal said she was chasing after a lost cat. Her parents didn't believe her excuse and, goodness, what a scolding she received in front of the rest of the attendees. She said the appropriate words and made the right movements, but out of the corner of our eyes, the three of us could tell she wasn't sorry in the slightest. The same, general incident happened a few weeks later. No matter how many apology letters they made Opal write, or how many times they detained her in her room, Opal hardly learned. She was so bold, so fascinating to us youngsters, even if her physical training regime was unoptimized, to put it charitably.

"The Satonos were determined to forge some manner of networking between our families via Opal's existing connection with us. At first, it was babysitting duty and lessons, but Opal didn't like those, so she often found an excuse or made a distraction to sneak us out and run in the family garden together. When she kept offending, our nannies threw up their hands, and the sessions became early race training together. We spent many colorful afternoons running amok in fake scrimmages and games. Did you know that whenever Ramonu's legs became too tired—she had issues as a small girl—Opal would piggyback her and run in her place?"

A vein in Oguri's forehead twitches. She can't decide if it's from amusement or shock. Ramonu would murder Rudolf, if she knew Rudolf were speaking these words.

"She also loved to sneak us snacks," Rudolf adds. She pinches her index and her thumb. Another bizarre sight. "Very unhealthy ones."

"She ran with you later on at Tracen, right?" Oguri says.

Rudolf's eyes lower, slightly. "You saw the old footage."

"The documentary about Opal showed her old interviews. One of them was about who'd end up as the biggest playmakers of the next generation. She mentioned you, Sirius and Ramonu," Oguri says.

"It was nothing special."

"The URA wouldn't see it that way, had Opal not done what she did."

"I suppose. She could've been the uma who trained the Emperor," Rudolf muses, "It has a nice mythological ring to it, a female Chiron or Merlin of sorts."

"She still got herself pregnant."

"Oh yes, that! We really laid into her. Ramonu was especially ornery about it, seeing as Opal just put her pursuit of the Satono dream on hold. Nothing was about to stop her from becoming the best mother ever, albeit a teenage, unprepared one about to suffer a dangerous delivery. Then, she succeeded. She was proud of that. And she still found time to repeat our childhood days in between her training for her first G1," Rudolf's smile has gone wistful, perhaps blissful. It vanishes. She touches a hand to the forehead. "And now: the elephant in the room."

Oguri nods again. One of Ruby's hecklers had dug through the URA archives and stitched together a reel of Rudolf's generation through various clips. Post the Satsuki-Sho, beneath a cold blue sky, a young and eager journalist ran up to ask Rudolf about how she felt about her very controversial former senpai. All joy drained from Rudolf's demeanor and her right hand vibrated, as if she were seconds from grabbing the microphone and bludgeoning the offending journalist with it. Mejiro Ramonu, in contrast at her Oka Sho, didn't entertain the question for a second.

Rudolf falls silent. Oguri opens her mouth to ask if she's okay, only to be dismissed by a quick wave of Rudolf's hand.

"I won't pretend Opal was the most important uma in my life. She'd have to compete with Speed Symboli, my cousin, Sirius, Ramonu and others. I don't enjoy such comparisons anyway. It still remains the fact that the senpai who tussled my hair, who presented me with her baby daughter and said the infant liked me, who told the entire world in a few years time, Sirius, Ramonu and I were about to blow everyone's minds with how powerful we were—she ruined the lives of two fellow contestants and violated the very foundation the URA is built upon," Rudolf says. She clasps her hands together, edging towards the seat's edge. "On live television, I cursed Opal. I told the crowd our past history was false; that we were never friends in the first place. No-one questioned me and I relished in my self-rightenousness. I truly, truly despised Opal with all my heart."

The atmosphere in the lavish office goes static, bordering on suffocating. Rudolf isn't glancing at her anymore. The shadows seem to wrap around her, concealing her expression. What little Oguri can see of it is truly twisted. She then tips her head back and laughs.

"And now her daughter is here! At my kingdom's own doorstep. How small our world is."

She follows it up with a sound, this mixture of a bitter chuckle mixed in with an exasperated gasp, layered with the timbre of the threatening tone she warned Oguri with long ago.

The pain from that day scabbed and scarred. It never truly healed. This is how the Emperor withdraws into herself, Oguri realises.

The rest is hard to contemplate. Because, this is Rudolf, unanimously-respected Symboli Rudolf, incorruptible champion of the URA, speaking, and she frames Opal as almost normal. As a person with her own life in the distant past; who laughed and sweated and ate snacks and probably had to calm the young Rudolf down from throttling her in a scene out of a domestic comedy show. Reconciling that alongside the monster in Oguri's wandering thoughts is...

A lump in her throat. She stares down at her shoes. She can't put the vibrations of her churning gut into words.

Rudolf glances out towards the gap in the curtains, where the faint sound of birdsong and umas playing flits behind the thick glass.

"One day, at no particular hour, I saw a particular, crumpled enrollment form on my desk, and it brought back those nostalgic days in a rush. Absence makes the hatred grow dimmer, it seems. And I began to think, as I did in those many dark days: 'if only'. If only someone had reached out to my senpai beforehand, or discovered the missing toolbox earlier, or by some miracle I had wandered lost, discovered her interrogation room, barged down the door with a kick and grabbed her and dragged her to a WcDonalds, where I'd have sat her down and demanded she explain herself for five seconds—" Rudolf inhales a breath. That wistful smile reappears, pained at the edges. "It's far too late now."

————

On a bright weekend day, Oguri stumbles across Ruby milling about in some second-rate shopping mall within Fuchu's center. Her immediate thought is to turn on her heel and leave Ruby alone. Problem is, Ruby's flitting about the place. She looks mildly lost. Grass, for some reason, decided that Ruby's weekends are none of her business.

So, Oguri approaches Ruby. Not to observe her, but to speak to her like a regular uma. Ruby is as receptive as ever. The two of them stroll around a sports equipment store, talking about the products on display. Oguri takes it upon herself to walk Ruby through the basics of buying proper shoes and cleats. The young girl knows little, as evidenced by her fondness for the energy drinks. It's an underground idol thing, isn't it? Oh, Ruby, no, please no—those drinks are slop in a tin can. They'll drag her down to the ground during a race. And then there's the artificial bullcrap corporations insist on disguising behind pretty graphic design logos. She can't drink those.

Nothing bad happens. No-one is hurt. The affair is as surreal as it is self tormenting. Oguri decides that, one, her apology letter needs revising, and two, she'll take Ruby to the best ramen place Oguri knows so that Ruby can taste a true Fuchu delicacy. It won't make up for what Oguri's misdeeds, but it'll be a start.

Satono Diamond arrives.

Oguri isn't impressed. The young uma can barely hide her disgust of Ruby behind her Satono-mandated mask of politeness. Her attempts to 'reconcile' are clearly attempts to wrench a legal statement out of her exiled sister. It's so transparent, so weaselly and pathetic, Oguri contemplates just piggybacking Ruby like Opal did with Ramonu and booking it out of the shopping mall entirely.

Ruby herself is rigid with danger signals. But, she chooses to go with Diamond against her better judgment. She has to, her expression screams.

Okay. Oguri's with her. Someone has to stay in Ruby's ballpark.

In a coffee house laden with stagnant opulence and too many expensive desserts, Diamond drops the facade and verbally assaults Ruby. Ruby's composure shatters. Oguri finds herself receiving questions she could never comprehend answering.

What do you mean Ruby has Opal's shoes?

What do you mean the Satonos wanted to burn those shoes?

What do you mean Ruby was locked in a shrine and forced to become a miko at the age of five after the Satonos separated her from her mom?

Oguri snaps out of it, just in time to hear Ruby's pleas falling on Diamond's deaf ears. The petulant girl looks at this display of pure compassion and spits in her exiled sister's face. Ruby slumps in her spot, her head lolling, like a puppet with its strings cut. In response, Diamond slams her palm on the table and demands Ruby look her in the eye.

The cutting knife weighs hot and heavy in Oguri's hand. She sees red.

————

Ruby sits on the park bench. The bottle of lemon tea Oguri practically tore out of a nearby vending machine rests between her hands, her grip so loose the bottle threatens to fall to the ground. Her head droops forward like a wilted sunflower.

And Oguri, who is next to her, breathless from running and having just belted out a frantic voice message to Grass, catches sight of those silent tears down blank cheeks.

Who is this girl? Oguri asks herself.

And—did I do this?

No, the lines etched on her naked palms seem to say, you were not Diamond. You did not spear Ruby through the chest. You did nothing. Never accepting, always watching. You sat by and let her defenses crumble to this point. Ruby might have never cried when faced against her hecklers, or when hearing her classmates whisper behind her back, and you were oblivious enough to think she couldn't possibly be worn down by such constant attacks. You could have welcomed her without bias, run laps with her, gone shopping, danced together, buffet hopped, crane machine dueled, introduced her to Belno and Kitahara and Tamamo and Creek and done a million other things that could've made her feel like a normal girl while letting the entire academy understand the Ashen Beast was standing with her alongside the second coming of Maruzensky, but you didn't; everything you did in exchange was wrong, and now this girl has collapsed to the state where she might not ever pick herself back up and that makes you the most despicable uma of them all.

Not knowing what else she can do, Oguri holds Ruby's hand and waits for Grass to arrive. She helps Ruby drink the lemon tea. She answers Grass's questions to help Grass understand, and when Ruby breaks down again, she holds the girl and nuzzles her like her own mother did when she was a lame, poor child. It is late, far too late, and it is the only apology Oguri can give.

————

"They don't dispose of the initial prototypes," Belno answers, "Because they might need to repurpose old designs for new ones. Opal's original plushie should be located in their storage."

(Do you forgive Oguri?)

[] I do, because it wasn't her fault.

[] I do, because she admitted her wrongdoing.

[] I do, because she gave me the plushie.

[] I don't, because she was like the rest.

[] I don't, because she hates my mother.

[] I don't, because I'm afraid of her now.

[] I can't answer that right now.

5.5: And Now

>>I will. On one condition. We do all that you wanted to do and we should've done. Properly, as friends this time.

>>Kitasan Black

>>Smart Falcon

Late Afternoon, July 7th, 20XX

[Mood has decreased to Good.]

Silence reigns in the wake of Oguri's tale, thick, tensile and suffocating. It's a lapse of consciousness where your ears and nerve endings strain themselves for a drop that never arrives. Oguri doesn't speak further, choosing to breathe in-and-out, in-and-out, on the bed she's collapsed on, so you take the initiative.

You shift the weight of your right foot, nudging an empty orange juice bottle that had fallen to the ground amidst your mounting shock and horror throughout the story.

The bottle clatters. Your tongue unglues and the imaginary tick-tocking ringing in your head finally ends.

"I thought you wanted to be my friend," you say.

Oguri doesn't reply at first. She gazes down at her lap, then speaks.

"I…that was the intention, yeah. What I wanted to do after I came to my senses."

"And before?" you ask. "Were any of those good intentions there before?"

"It was for…" Oguri swallows, the motion visible, the sound audible. "It was for getting close to you, so that I could, y'know, as I described, see you for who you were. In the end, I guess I failed."

She failed. She failed.

You blink. Something lashes upwards inside of your abdomen, hot and violently slick as old wok oil, and you almost burst out laughing. She failed. Yes, that's an accurate summary, isn't it? She, Oguri Cap, famous, world-renowned Oguri Cap, failed. She's admitted it flat to your face. Had someone told you that statement before today, you would've politely smiled at best or mocked them to their face, because the idea of an uma so successful, so privileged and promising, having failed in any real capacity in any stage of her life would be ludicrous.

Today, it seems, is a day for bowling your brain over like it's fifty percent off at the local alley.

The best part, you think with a hysterical internal giggle, is that Oguri didn't fail her master's degree or some other important grown-up task. She failed in assessing you. The charade of superimposing your mother's sins atop your soul, the same cherry-picking of 'evidence', the persistence and buckling down when reality shook its head and refused to entertain her conclusion—it was all there. Same old, same old.

She could have asked. You would've given an answer. Instead, she assumed you would…what, exactly? Bite her head off? Rip your face off and unleash the so-called evil of Satono Opal from within? You don't know. You simply understand she acted like Duo Pelte, like those paparazzi who made you disguise yourself when you went out, like those bullies whom Oguri confronted not even half a day ago. Those people wished you would suffer.

"I told my old friends about you."

Oguri looks up. "Pardon?"

Somewhere amidst your thoughts, you tilt your head backwards. The ceiling light shines down. The tugging at the sides of your mouth informs you it's carved into a sardonic smile, but the heaviness clinging to your eyes speaks of the irises losing their light. Beneath them, the thin lining of flesh atop your neck bulges.

"I told my old friends about you," you repeat, your own voice sounding distant, the vocal cords puppeteered by some ghostly apparition. "The ones from my old idol unit. Tomorrow is FAITHFUL. Does the name ring a bell?"

"They're from the underground scene, right? People discovered them online," Oguri says. Her stare lands firmly on your exposed neck. "They do enka. That's why I introduced you to Inari."

"Ah, so that was why. I wondered about that. Same for Super Creek, Tamamo, Ardan and the others, right? Makes sense. Makes sense." you say. You then wave your hand quickly, dismissively. "They're not whom I'm interested in talking about right now."

Oguri makes a stuttering sound.

"You had your chance to talk, so it's my turn now, capiche?"

"I…" Oguri says. "Sure."

"Okay. Saya was your fan."

"Who?"

"Saya. One of FAITHFUL's members. The sleepy yet competent type. You know, like Seiun Sky. It's their brand. When I told her, Saya, that I had met the Oguri Cap and ran with her in my first ever race, she was over the moon, then greener than a fresh lime with envy. She wouldn't stop pestering me for details. Grass Wonder was famous for winning the Takarazuka and stuff recently back then—but you? The Oguri Cap?" You lift your head back, tone switching to a drawl. "The whole office spat out their drinks in a double take."

That's not a joke. You still have the photo of the office break room on your phone. A full slab of varnished wood soaked in splatters of cheap cola and breakfast milk.

"Saya woke up on the spot. Chugged two Umonsters down and grabbed me for a call. She told me I'd stumbled on a one-in-a-million chance, how respected and important you still were to the scene after you raced. How your words were still taken seriously by commentary casters and aspiring umas. She kept messaging me with these tips about networking and making friends with celebs she picked up at university. All of them— Kaede, my old Manager, Hotaru, Miki. Everyone. At random times of the day, within random LANE chatrooms we'd set up between each other. Half of the tips from there never ended up being used, since Grass kept me uber-busy due to my catch-up training, but it didn't matter. We were that excited, because I thought it meant that my Tracen career was starting off on a great note."

Throughout your entire speech, Oguri's complexion has kept paling, her mouth shut tightly.

You shrug, slowly and with exaggeration. "Guess it wasn't what I thought it was, huh?"

Oguri pushes herself towards the edge of the bed. She stands up. Her body jerks forward, a desperate gasp launching itself out of her mouth. She mimes with her hands towards your disinterested self.

"It wasn't all fake."

"Oh, was it?"

"The time in that coffee house, where that spoiled brat of an ex-sister harassed you—that was real. I couldn't stand her rich girl attitude and how she hurt you with those passive-aggressive barbs and demanded your mother's shoes. I chose to defend you. That was real!"

You remember. Back then, you'd been secretly grateful through the wall of grief that Oguri was there. It feels far away now, tainted with an undercurrent of doubt. Or was that fake, too? Is this another ploy of yours? Such questions run through your mind.

[Alignment: Dark < 10 || Chaos < 10]

They do not vocalize.

They must show on your face. Oguri continues.

"And, prior to that, I was going to apologise. I thought about leaving you alone and minding my own business, but you looked lost in the sports store and I was afraid you'd get scammed by some plastic-smiled clerk. I genuinely enjoyed teaching you about nutritional supplements and the equipment back then. There was even a letter. It's…" Oguri glances around her room. "It's somewhere under the papers."

You are unconvinced.

"It got lost in the shuffle and the emergency back home. I didn't want to wait this long, but things kept getting in the way." Oguri splutters. "That's why I got the gift. My feelings are sincere. You have to…" Oguri's hands fall to her sides. "You gotta believe me."

The measly tone she speaks in makes you wonder if someone in her life said it before. And it is more irksome than it has any right to be.

"You could've asked me." you say, "You and everyone else could've asked me what I was planning."

"I know. We should have," Oguri says.

"Like, I'm not stupid. I'm aware of the controversy surrounding my mom. I knew there'd be a ruckus when word of my enrolment leaked out. Detecting when people love or hate me—that's my job as an umadol. And even if I wasn't an umadol, this finding-out, true-self revealing has been the bill whenever I work for a few months and my boss looks into me and discovers my real name." You shake your head. Your nails dig into the sides of your naked flesh, as you fold your arms. "Why else did I go straight to Rudolf on my first day? It was to show good faith. Tracen was the academy of my dreams and, honestly, I never once expected it to be any different."

"We were wrong," Oguri bemoans. "All of us. Everything we did. We shouldn't have compared you to your mother. You didn't deserve that!"

Something lurches inside of you, jutting out into a hot spike of pure rage.

[Composure Check: 83/100 -> Failure.]

"Would it kill any of you to see my mother as an actual person for five goddamn seconds?" you scream.

Oguri recoils at your outburst, the back of her knees whacking into the side of her bed. She stumbles, flails her arms, and falls on her bottom with a soft, dull thump. She gazes up with this meek, wallflower-esque posture that you remember from Rice Shower, from Tabaru under stress. Whereas upon two umas it is endearing, perhaps adorable, on Oguri it is enraging.

You're struck by the urge to grab her shoulders and shake the sensibility out of her frame. The monologue writes itself in your head. Tell me, please. Did I really look that scary to everyone? Me? These lips, this smile? Do I seriously look that much like the mom I've never met ever since I was five?

But Oguri isn't in the mood to answer. Look at her, wired up, ears pinned back, instinctively reacting as if a fight will break out. She's afraid of you.

The realisation roots you to the spot, elicits another bitter laugh, and floods you with a monumental soreness.

You can't do this.

You simply can't.

You don't enjoy it, you know? Learning the truth about people you thought liked your company, then exploding or ranting in their faces. Asking yourself where you went wrong, re-learning and re-affirming that there exist men who are pigs, women who are just the same, and the rest of the scum in between. It is so, so tiresome, and so utterly dreadful.

You slump back against the wall, glaring down at your shoes. You remember you're still holding onto Oguri's gift via the bow.

Oguri springs to life as you hold it up. "Wait. Please, Ruby, don't throw that away! What's inside is—"

Her own door slams in her face.

[Mood has dropped to Normal.]

The world is full of delectable smells, canvases of bright colors and wide open spaces where umas can race to their hearts' content. You wish you could lather it in gasoline and set it ablaze.

[World Resonance check: 110/55 -> Success! Trivial: +0 EXP.]

You settle for avoiding them instead.

As you lope down a circuit of the academy's outer fringe, you steam. Oguri Cap. Oguri freaking Cap. Say her name enough times, and the name becomes not a name and more of a jumble of syllables that hiss and fizz like coffin motel television static. She lied to you. She defended you. She hated you. She rescued you from your awful, awful estranged sister and her stupid friend, then had the gall to dump that on your head against your will.

It's a good afternoon to contemplate sudden inexplicable career changes. You wish you could be a neurosurgeon and rip the answer out of her head. Write a million-dollar-selling novel with the title How the Ashen Beast Screwed Me Over! Maybe a psychologist, adept in piecing together conclusions out of endless conversations, or not, since that one psychologist umafluencer on Umatok was spilling big fat lies.

Ooh, you recite inside your head with that faux-enthusiastic clinical tone nurses employ worldwide. By definition every entity with a beginning possesses an end. Ooh, bad moods are linked to hormones—therefore they can't last forever. Ooh, aah, erm, by the law of entropy the brain eventually tires of screaming and thrashing and will eventually shut itself down.

Well, you'd wish your cere-this or hypo-whatever would hurry up and do its job.

[Mood has dropped to Bad.]

It's tempting to throw Oguri's gift into the nearest trash can. The underground umadol inside you, who never once refused a gift, won't allow it.

You end up slumped spread-eagle on the grass. Dandelion particles blow. The grass, green grass smiles, and that reminds you that thanking Grass for saving your rear needs to be jotted down on your itinerary. Get her a big matcha birthday cake, if you don't want to frighten her to death. That's far off in the future, in some nebulous afterstate in which you've cooled down and can muster the enthusiasm to thank Grass properly. Best not to drag Grass into menhera-town.

You sneeze. Spots dance in your eyes. Two voices float downstream.

"And then Nase took out her glowsticks and pushed her way to the front of the crowd towards the front stage and—"

"She did? The Trainer Nase held those?"

"She did! Everyone around her was so surprised, me the most. But she was totally serious and into the wotagei. She didn't have to, but she did for me! It was incredibly sweet of her. I gave her the biggest hug backstage afterwards."

You groan out loud. Middle finger to the Three Goddesses with a restraining order on top. You are not in the mood to deal with these two right now.

Kitasan Black and Smart Falcon do not hear your internal pleas and wander across like the morons they are, right as you're picking yourself up to skedaddle out of the place.

Standing a few feet away, they stare, their mouths dangling from mid-conversation. Kitasan is in her sports gear, whereas Smart Falcon is dolled up in her uniform. You stare back.

Your estranged sister's best friend along with the rival umadol who has consistently sneered and stuck out her tongue at you, like some preschooler whenever the two of you run across each other in the halls. Fantastic. This is the exact opposite of a comforting shoulder to cry on.

A cool breeze carrying a stray leaf blows through the gap between you and them.

"Ruby," Kitasan says. "Um, er…hi?"

"Hello, Kitasan," you respond flatly. This is the first real time you've exchanged words with her since tryouts. Unlike that time, you're in no mood to wave hands and exchange pleasantries. "Is Dia nearby?"

"No. I mean, I don't think so?" Kitasan replies. She glances behind her, shifting her weight from one foot to the other. A soaked towel hangs around her neck, evidence of a fresh workout.

"Oh," you reply. "That's a first."

"She has meetings with her Trainer around that time, so I'm often by myself around these times, if I'm not with my own team. It's not as if we were born joined at the hip! As for Smart Falcon, we sort of ran into each other and recognised each other as music lovers and began chatting so…" The gesture Kitasan gives to Smart Falcon goes floppy in the face of your complete disinterest.

"Sorry to interrupt, but is this drama I shouldn't be intruding on?" Smart Falcon speaks up.

You turn to her.

Smart Falcon's thin eyebrows press together. Her twin hazelnuts of eyes squint amidst her gorgeous complexion and oval face and golly gee, does she look good today? Classic aboveground umadol aesthetic. Classic mainstream beauty standards, in which you either dress up as if a camera is ready around the nearest corner or you don't leave the changing room at all.

Knowing her, she's wearing her idol dress beneath her academy uniform. Barf.

"Nah," you reply.

"That took a while," Smart Falcon comments.

"There a problem?" you ask.

"I don't know, Ruby. Does it often take you that long to answer a question with a single word?"

Is she trying to needle you until you bleed?

"This is nothing either of you needs to be concerned with."

"The way you're speaking is sorta implying the other way," Smart Falcon says.

She instinctively moves to the side of Kitasan, as if shielding her with the barest portion of her elbow. You scowl.

"Are you picking a fight with me, Falco? You wanna throw down on the track."

Smart Falcon flinches, taken aback. "Wha—excuse you? Where did that come from?"

"My lack of patience. You see, I just had an appointment where I was trauma dumped upon in a fashion that has driven a nail into my skull, giving me the worst headache in the world, which means I have no urge to fluff up your ego today, alright?"

"It was an honest question!" Smart Falcon exclaims.

"Are you okay?" Kitasan asks.

She says those words in earnest, with such puppy-dog curiosity that an outside observer would mistake her for a friend of yours. The mere idea causes your throat to burn with a vile acid. Right, right. Diamond isn't present. That means Kitasan can actually care for a change. She can behave like an uma with her own thoughts and initiative, instead of a trembling bonsai tree with ropes in her hair. How much money did her daddy pay to suck up to the Satonos, by the way?

"Please leave me alone," you respond.

"Hey—"

You cut Smart Falcon off before she protests further. "Same for you, Falco. It's what's mutually best for the both of us. Leave me alone. Go back to singing on stage and gaining one trillion fans or whatever it is real umadols do. It's not as if you thought me one anyway."

You turn on your heel and trudge off, glaring at the grass as you do so. Behind you, you hear an intake of breath.

"Stop."

It's Smart Falcon.

You groan out loud. Seriously? For real? You resume your walk.

"I said stop, Satono Ruby!"

The usage of your full name, along with the shout that explodes from Smart Falcon's lungs, startles you. Your tail jolts up. Confused, and still miffed, you whirl around and see Smart Falcon less than half a meter before you, hands on her hips and her cheeks puffed up. She whips out a finger, the tip an invisible straight line from your nose.

"Excuse me—"

"Repeat that again," Smart Falcon demands.

"Repeat what?" you ask.

"The thing you just said. The stuff about me not seeing you as a real umadol!" Smart Falcon exclaims.

"I…you said it yourself!"

"Congratulations, Ruby," Smart Falcon huffs. "That is the most offensive thing I've heard all day."

You boggle at her. Sorry. Did you hear that correctly? You're the offensive uma here?

Smart Falcon sees you don't understand and launches into an explanation.

"Do you understand how many umadols are enrolled in Tracen? Think about it. Think very hard about what that title means," Smart Falcon says. She pulls her finger back, and sweeps her arms around. A heavy dose of premonition hits you, and you open your mouth to interrupt. It's too late. Smart Falcon drops her voice, going deeper, more resonant, sonorous. It's as if an invisible audience has manifested around her, with you and Kitasan at the forefront.

"It's not the number of girls who've sung in a Winning Live out of contractual obligation. It's not the number who sing on the stage as a hobby or spend hours in a karaoke booth. I'm talking about umas who actually pay more than five seconds of their attention to the music industry. Who listen to the newest hits and critique them while organizing their penlights. I'm talking about umas who live for the moment those blazing hot lights flicker on and the intro riff plays, the pose and movements they've practiced a hundred times in the mirror already surging their way up their nerves to create the most splendid, the most spectacular and awesome opening act in all of Tracen!"

You find yourself nodding along, to your horror. This is umadol talk. Nutrients to your underground umadol brain. Smart Falcon is repeating the reasons you persisted in your umadol career, despite Tomorrow is FAITHFUL's setbacks, the arduous demand for self-discipline, the schedule so tightly packed that public holidays became special work days, and conditions that led Kaede to slug down paracetamol while sick just so she could finish an all-nighter concert and give back to her fans.

You understand completely. Except for the reason why Smart Falcon is ranting to you about this now.

"How many umadols are enrolled in Tracen?" Smart Falcon asks.

"Uh…" Kitasan stammers.

"Two?" you reply.

Smart Falcon flashes the V-sign with her fingers. "Two. Two umadols. You and me."

"And…?"

"What do you mean 'and'? Do you have any clue how hard I tried to find another umadol other than us?"

"…why would you do that?"

"Because it's lonely at the top! A summit isn't a summit when there's barely a mountain!" Smart Falcon explodes at you. She clenches her fist, looking pained. "I tried to find other members. Other peers to the umadol dreams. Silence Suzuka. I admit, she came a little close, but it was always obvious running was her one true love. She flew to America, in the end, leaving me high and dry. There was that new rookie, Mihono Bourbon—I thought I could interest her with the idea of preparing for the Winning Live. But she's not great at expression and her Trainer was way too intimidating! Agnes Tachyon was my last hope—"

"Tachyon? The mad scientist Agnes Tachyon?" Kitasan interjects.

"Not my best idea, but she talked a big game about surpassing the limits of an uma's body, including those of dancing and singing. She wanted to research how the Winning Live helps us grow and run. But she got arrested by campus security for strange smells coming from her lab and lost interest after that!"

A choke escapes from Smart Falcon. It's hard not to imagine a single tear pouring down those round cheeks.

"That's why! That's exactly why!" Smart Falcon points at you again, her arm stretched firm and straight. "You—Satono Ruby! You listen to me! I refuse to stand there and let the only other umadol in this academy denigrate herself into a regular—no, worse than a regular uma. I deny your denial of yourself!"

Flames coat her body from head to toe as her eyes shine with the blinding force of fresh stars. You have to remind yourself this is Smart Falcon's soul radiating forth. She's not about to cook herself charred.

She then grabs you by the wrist.

"Hey!" you exclaim.

"There's no time to waste. We need to go," Smart Falcon says.

"Go where?"

"To fix that mentality of yours."

"It was a figure of speech!" You yank your wrist away. "Don't touch me!"

"You said it, which means you were considering it! C'mon!"

She grabs you again and begins pulling. You give up and relinquish control to your legs, letting yourself be carried along for the ride. Your shoes dig across the concrete. Passersby stare, but Smart Falcon drags you past before they can form a coherent thought. Whatever, you think. Why not? You're already reeling, seeing chirping birds and circling stars, from the morning's events. What's another inexplicable diversion?

Kitasan trails behind you all.

Smart Falcon's destination ends up being an outdoor practice arena. There are a couple of them in the academy. They're arena-style dome-roofed installations, located in a minor amphitheater dug into the soil, with each stage supported by two thick pillars at the edges of the large acting area. The architecture is nothing amazing. Solid brick-colored installations, with rows of wooden benches making up the audience's seating. They're good enough to get the job done and to hold events in, and that's what matters.

When you first practiced on one in your first week—alone—you marvelled at how wide-reaching the floor space was alongside how efficiently the architecture amplified your acoustics. You'd love to sing with the rest of FAITHFUL or a couple of your old rivals on one of these stages, or perhaps a new friend of yours, even if the outdoor nature means performances can get chilly in the later months. You never thought your partner would be Smart Falcon, of all umas.

Smart Falcon disappears into the stage's rear. She returns, hauling a CD player. She slams the machine down, crouches near it and inserts a CD from her bag. A click of a button, and the machine kicks off a backing track.

She then reaches further into her bag, stands up, and hands you a microphone.

"Sing," she orders you.

"Excuse me?"

"C'mon, sing!" Smart Falcon impatiently nudges your microphone in your direction. "You feel like crap, don't you?"

You look at the microphone's monochrome diaphragm, then at Smart Falcon. "Hold on, are you trying to cheer me up?"

She rolls her eyes. "Yes, duh!"

You're speechless.

"What sort of umadol would I be if I noticed a girl in distress and kept on walking? An absolutely terrible one. Now, sing! You gotta stop thinking so hard sometimes," Smart Falcon replies.

You don't answer, because you think your mental faculties are short-circuiting.

The backing track bleats into full swing at this point. Smart Falcon jerks away from you. She hops on the spot, landing with her feet a shoulder length apart. She winks to the audience, which consists of Kitasan only, flashes a V-sign near one eye and launches into the first verse with gusto.

Immediately, your face scrunches up. Oh goddesses. Oh no. That upbeat tempo, those high-pitched vocals amidst the synths. The sound of handclaps and bright guitars with bells. Put the pieces together, and hey, presto, it's an aboveground mainstream girly-pop song!

You shouldn't have expected anything else from Smart Falcon. And yet—does it have to sound this generic? It's like she took a robot, fed it a hundred chart-toppers and withdrew the result after the poor machine got its gears clogged with an onslaught of cotton candy and sugar diabetes stardust. The lyrics aren't any better. The chorus extols the virtues of 'doing your best!' and 'never giving up!' before switching into a segment about 'a bright and happy umadol day!' The song is so much more sickeningly cheery than the loudest Winning Live songs, which at least have the decency to extol your favorite sport.

Your right eyebrow twitches so fiercely it threatens to detach from its follicles. The aboveground idol scene was a mistake. All that mainstream attention has dried up the creative matter in its idols' brains.

But.

The more you listen to the cheery garbage, the more you acclimatize to it. The more you are unable to deny that Smart Falcon pulls the song off. Her voice is high-pitched and energetic to match the backing track, yet maintains a smooth cadence, never sliding off-tempo. She hits the high notes without cracking. It's obvious she's practiced this song in private. The umadol inside of you finds her technical prowess impressive, personal opinions aside.

Your foot, the traitorous appendage, taps itself along to the beat.

Smart Falcon notices. Without breaking her stride, she cricks her neck and flashes you a smirk. It instantly pisses you off. That's right. This is the umadol who dogged on the entire Tomorrow is FAITHFUL by singing enka in your face.

The previous hours vanish into nothingness as heat floods back into your limbs.

The heck are you lolling about the stage for? You're no coward. You can give Smart Falcon as good as she gave you. So what if the music isn't your preferred genre? You're a professional. Sucking it up and adjusting to the client's requests is your job.

[Mood has increased to Normal.]

Squeezing a fist, you march up towards Smart Falcon as the song fades, and step into position side by side.

Bring it on, says your terse nod at her.

She glances at you, her smirk growing. Like you stand a chance.

Curfew's happening in thirty, the audience is a single confused Team Spica member, and the album on the CD player blasts the sort of slop you spent many lovely late nights trashing on LANE with Hotaru. It's more than enough. The next song comes on, a fluffy-sounding opening track with a singer lapsing midway into her cotton-candy dreams, and Smart Falcon launches into her dance.

When she steps right, you step right. When she clicks her heels, you click yours. She raises her hand, bobbing her arm up and down as she flexes her fingers, and you watch her until the final moment, then snap your own hand into a predicted palm sign. It ends up being the correct one. Your eyes flash with glee.

See that, Falco? You can improvise, too. It's a tricky business, since a good deal of it is impulse-based, but you studied common patterns and dance theory in the spaces where you should've been attending middle school.

Thanks to your own prowess, you endure the stupid aboveground backing track to not vomit inside your own head. You manage to copy Falcon…

[Dancing check: 123/180 -> Failure.]

…but you don't outshine her.

It's execrable, admitting this, but, as a professional, you gotta keep it real. First of all, don't get it twisted. You're good. Perhaps this competition was malformed from the beginning, considering she's playing songs you barely lent an ear to until now. The music industry, however, doesn't care two hoots for what is fair. It wouldn't exist, otherwise.

Here's the truth. Smart Falcon has broken past the skill ceiling you're still climbing towards. Her superiority lies in the subtle motions: the lack of jerkiness as she skips side by side. The balance in her hips as she sways and twirls, never letting one side of her body rise too high, nor dip too low. The sheer synchronicity between her singing and her motor controls. Her anatomy flows like water sliding down a mountain stream. One song slaps down a rapid beat that doesn't seem to end. Where you trip and stumble over a few lyrics, slipping your smile in the process, Smart Falcon juggles her voice, her posture and her cheer without dropping a single one.

For the final insult, she exits her dance with aplomb, dropping into a confident pose, then a two-handed wave. I hope to see you again! her waving, cheery hands say, and dazzle the crowd. There's zero hesitation about which of you the hypothetical audience will remember more.

Smart Falcon deserves her reputation. Her thousands of views and umadol brand deals. Kaede would act starstruck in front of her—a thought that sends you fuming. And smiling.

"Had enough?" Smart Falcon asks.

"You wish!" you exclaim. The feeling brimming in your chest—it's the exact same razor-edged euphoria from the finale of a long concert, or a close race with Tabaru. The fires of competition swell, hot and loud. You want to slam down FAITHFUL's tracks into that CD player, amp up the volume, and challenge Smart Falcon to an enka rematch. This time, she won't catch you off guard.

Nature has other ideas.

A cold wind blows. You whip your head forward. The horizon stretching the skyline has grown grayer, darker. The air, colder. A bite of chill hits your knees and you shiver.

Smart Falcon notices. Your eyes meet. An unspoken truce is made.

"But you win, for now," you say.

Any further exercise in this weather, and you run the risk of growing sick. You're not so addled as to forget your debut.

"You mean, I win forever~" Smart Falcon teases back. "Because, while you've improved—no really—so have I. And I just won't stop."

You don't doubt it. Smart Falcon wouldn't be Tracen's top dirt racer, if she weren't one determined uma.

So what?

You don't care about that, just as she doesn't care you're Satono Opal's daughter. The idea fills you with another dose of competition's high. Straightening your back, you whip out your own finger and point at her.

"You better not rest on your laurels, Falco. I'm the girl who rose from complete uma running pauper to almost beating little Miss Spica over there. The last batch of umas who underestimated me paid for it."

"And you think that talk gives you power over me?" Smart Falcon says.

You smirk. "You just showed me your moves. I've already got a plan brewing in my head. One day, you'll look back on this and consider it the worst mistake you ever made."

The plan is already hatching in your head. Once you challenge more umas to dance-offs…

The feeling, you presume from the giggle she lets out, is mutual.

As you drink, you catch Kitasan staring at you.

"Nothing." Kitasan glances to the side. Halfway through the performance, she stood up, cheering and pumping fists throughout the song, a scene that must've looked insane to anyone watching from afar. Now, she seems abashed. Faintly ashamed of herself. "Good work."

[Psyche meter has increased by 5%.]

Your dorm room greets you like a warm, slightly fuzzy sweater. After shutting the door and locking it, you flop down on your bed and bury yourself in your pillow, all without bothering to remove your uniform.

What a day. What an absolute washing-machine spinning hurricane of a day. From visiting the last of Oguri's pals, to stopping her from beating the snot out of those bullies, to hearing her tale, getting pissed and concluding by dancing with Smart Falcon of all things. Less than twenty-four hours have passed, yet the block of time has felt like several weeks.

You can't fall asleep now. Dinner's waiting, then homework. The world doesn't stop because you're the most exhausted you've been since Grass's personal boot camp.

A ten-minute power nap should be fine, though. You let your eyes flutter shut and grant your mind permission to slide into the blackness.

When you wake up, twenty minutes have passed, according to the clock. A trickle of drool trails down the side of your mouth. Rolling over, a sharp corner digs into your side.

Oguri's gift. Somehow, it wasn't lost in the confusion. Somehow, you remembered, consciously or not, to grab it from place to place.

You pick it up. The wrapping has somehow stayed intact. The colors haven't lost their sheen. It's tempting to hurl it into the room's bin once more, but, again, you refuse.

You've cooled down. You comprehend that 1. You'd have to explain to Tabaru, who might unwrap it—she is a Gold uma, after all. 2. The duty of an umadol to open all non-explosive gifts still holds. 3. You can comprehend without scowling that Oguri was telling the truth. She was being genuine when she defended you from Diamond. No-one threatens to amputate an ex-sister's index and middle fingers if they didn't care about someone. Had Oguri not been there, backing you up and escorting you out, you might've fallen into a pit and never climbed back out, possibly ending in you leaving Tracen for good.

You're not as furious at Oguri anymore. Still peeved, to be sure, but not furious. The situation isn't as black-and-white as it first seemed. The spike of anger has dulled into a nub. The power nap, along with the prior dancing, reset the dials on your emotional state, it seems. You'd be planning to gift Smart Falcon a fruit basket, if you didn't view her music tastes with contempt.

4. Your silver bullet is reacting to it once more. Vibrating, spinning on its axis. It's consistent with when you first held the gift box.

Can inanimate objects latch onto a person and follow them from place to place? You'd say surely not, but it wasn't long ago you were attacked by evil shadow umas and conjured fire from your fingertips. Another entry in the list of questions to pester Plain Jane with the next time you meet.

You shake the gift. No loud noises come from within. Satisfied, you pull the bow and open the gift.

A doll rests in the box. An URA-brand Cutie, judging from the wrapping paper, and the uma ears. You pick it up, holding it to the light.

It's a doll of you.

You look again.

Nope. Nothing's changed. It's still a doll of you. Head size, eye color, jet-black, straight-cut hair, they're all present. The proportions are squished down and inflated, but that's standard for the chibified URA Cuties. Your first impression is confusion. It's unclear why Oguri thought a doll of yourself would cheer you up. Does she believe you to be a narcissist?

Then, you shift downwards, and examine the doll's clothing. The doll is clad in a costumed military outfit, the type you'd see in dramatic war or politics stage plays and anime. Running your fingers across the fabric, you brush across the over-the-shoulder black cape, then guide them down to the sleeveless vest-style bodice. A double row of decorative gold buttons lines the maroon front. Touches of golden embroidery line the front skirt, with black bows adorning the bottom.

It's G1 racewear, alright. A darker, more opulent counterpart to your own racewear. Rather handsome and elegant, befitting of a dark heroine in an action movie. Your confusion gives way to mild admiration. The doll isn't still you.

So who is this?

You haven't debuted yet. It is impossible for you to have earned a Cutie. Jordan told you that the racer and her Trainer need to sit down in front of a production committee to discuss merchandising rights and distribution. Standard marketing talk.

Which uma looks like you, and is also not you?

Your mind goes blank.

[(Logic check: 95/20) || (Wits check: 10/4) -> Success! Trivial: +0 EXP.]

The obvious answer crashes into you like a lightning bolt.

No. No, no, NO—

Stop—

That's ridiculous—

They recalled the majority of those dolls and incinerated them in the Satonos' furnaces. The remnants were lost or locked up in private collectors' galleries. Tracen students are prestigious, but not that prestigious.

However, your mind says as it ticks on, if you were as famous as the Oguri Cap, you'd possess so many connections in the industry, and since you'd still be famous, those corporations and agencies would practically trip over themselves to plaster your name on their products in exchange for a piece of cloth—

The ground threatens to bottom out beneath your feet.

Breathing hard, you twist the doll over. You almost drop it, fingers colliding into each other. You find the label at the back where the specifications, along with the doll's namesake, are located.

You read it, and suddenly, you're not breathing. You're hyperventilating.

"Mom." Your voice comes out as a shaky whine. You raise the doll up to the pale ceiling light with shaking hands. The pale luminescence shines down and around the doll's oversized head, obscuring its form, save for its face, its cheeky stitched grin shining back, evergreen and pristine.

"Mom. Mom, Mom, Mom!"

Tears threaten to pour out from the corner of your squeezed eyes. You tell yourself that this can't be real. This has to be a dream. A dream conjured up by your childhood dreams and the delirium of a once-broken forehead. The doll does not vanish, however, no matter how many times you count to ten, nor when you bite down on the inside of your mouth and try to draw blood.

The doll of your lost mother exists and it's real in your hands.

You fall backwards onto your bed. The tears fall, salty and raw. You smash your face into your pillow before any of them fall onto the doll's head and ruin its hair.

"Mom. You're here. You're finally, finally here with me."

You curl up, hugging and stroking and whispering sweet nothings you won't recall towards the doll. A bewildered laugh escapes you, which elicits a delighted sob in exchange. Your heart flutters with ecstasy, purer than any stimulant, lighter than any post-concert shakes. All the while, your silver bullet dances on its chain, its vibrations sending a beautiful fuzziness through your chest.

Oguri—

How did she fetch this? What sort of favors did she have to call in to find the last of the Satono Opal dolls? No, you correct yourself, not just one of the last few unburned, non-destroyed dolls. She procured the original prototype. That's an apex piece of merchandise, the rarest of the rare, and it's so pristine, so fresh-smelling, it could've come straight out of the designer's hands.

Oguri took great care in handling your mother's doll. She must've cradled it like a newborn child on her way back.

She betrayed your trust, then she fetched you a memento of the woman you've searched your entire life for.

You want to hug Oguri. Slap her in the face for leading you on a wild goose chase. Pester her about how she found the doll and if there are any other pieces of merch in reserve. You want to hug your mother's doll to breaking point, cuddle it to bits, commission Seamstress Sugar for more copies, learn sewing yourself, spend the last reserves of your bank account on the biggest, most metallic safe in existence and place it inside where no-one can touch it. If anyone breaks it, you'll destroy them.

Darkness clouds your eyes and you reaffirm yourself. Tabaru, Hishi Amazon, even the Prez—no-one is allowed to touch your mother's doll without your explicit permission. You almost crushed a man's skull when he tried to steal your mother's shoes. The same deal applies here.

Then, you let out a screech of joy and leap around, holding the doll in your arms, giggling and cooing and crying, as if you're the mother and it is the child.

Night falls. You make plans to find a good secure spot for the doll. For the time being, you hide it under your blankets. Sorry, Tabaru. She's a nice girl and a great roommate, but like many others, she acts uncomfortable when the topic of your mother is brought up.

When you go to sleep, you wrap the doll in your arms and smile.

That night, you have a dream.

A regular dream, far away from the Nightmare.

The sun shines, gentle and warm. Cicadas chirp through the summer sky. A wide-brimmed hat balances on your precarious little head, and the bottle of carrot juice in your hands is almost empty. You don't care, because bouncing on your sandals across this little dirt road is a delight, and your mother's hand in yours grips firm and tight.

She speaks, a finger to her lips. The words are silent, yet the meaning is clear. Today is a rest day. A day where the pressures of the Satono conglomerate and the drudgery of your homeschooled lessons shall be put on hold. It is a day for fun and games and many homemade snacks, and it shall happen in her favorite spot in the forest near the Satono manor.

The spot was once her little secret, and when you grow up, it shall be bequeathed and become yours. For now, eat these carrot sandwiches.

You glance up through the stray beams of light. Your mother's face is clear as day.

She has a kind smile.

Afternoon, July 8th, 20XX

"Oguri."

Oguri glances up from the bench she's sitting on. Dark rings circle her eyes. "Ruby, I—"

"I unwrapped your gift." you say.

Whatever words Oguri was about to speak die on her tongue. She cannot decide whether to stare at her shoes like the fool she believes herself to be, or meet your eyes in the proper show of respect.

You shrug. "It's hard to stay mad at someone when they gave me the last remaining doll of my mother."

"It—" Oguri's voice grinds out through her trembling. "It wasn't supposed to be like that. I didn't mean it. Everything I did was wrong. I didn't mean to hurt anybody, least of all an innocent girl like you!"

"I know," you say softly.

"If I could go back—I keep making these mistakes by putting my foot in my mouth! I don't understand what road of life I walked down to end up like this. I'm just so, so stupid!" Oguri cries. She curls her fingers, as if ready to claw out her own eyes.

Instead, she wilts on the bench, seemingly more defeated than she had been after the losses in her heyday. It's a sight that'd cause fainting spells amongst her diehard fans. In a sense, they contributed to the root of her problem. They built a narrative of an indomitable, incorruptible, do-no-wrong hero, and once she bought into it and tried to act the part, she ran into the shortcomings she suppressed so hard in that interim. period between her retirement and the present.

Perhaps, there's an argument to be made that she should've known better. She is older than you, after all. Perhaps, you are still annoyed that she thinks poorly of your mother. But if you severed connections based on that, you'd never make friends at all.

The anger, the spite, inside you has diminished. That is a good thing.

You walk over and sit down next to Oguri. "You did something wrong, then apologised for it. It might've been super convoluted and frankly disturbing—Grass was right to lay into you—but you still did it. It's more than most of my bullies have done. Thank you, Oguri. I appreciate it."

Oguri lifts her head, disbelieving.

"I'm sorry for snapping at you, too," you finish.

Pure relief releases the tension from her shoulders. She wipes an arm across her face, surely hiding the tears. You hear a sniffle.

You extend your hand. "Wanna be friends?"

Oguri grabs a tissue from her pocket and scrubs her fingers clean. She gingerly reaches out, testing her own volition, before she takes your hand and shakes it with a solid firmness.

"I'd be honored."

No further words are necessary. This is what should have happened from the very beginning.

Come to my office immediately. Don't speak a single word to others or touch any social media.

You're glad to have an excuse to ditch class, however.

Your teacher raises her spectacles. She beckons you wordlessly. You show her the message and, after a few seconds of reading, she shakes her head and lets you go. She holds zero authority here. This is a racing academy after all.

You fast-walk through the academy halls, keeping your head straight whilst eying the rest of the classrooms as you pass. Most of the other girls are focused on their studies. The ones procrastinating or in between classes with their own phones out—their stares linger on you. Whispers rise up.

Your heart pounds. You pick up the pace.
